Darby gets $450, he was born September 20, 1879, and he was appointed July 27, 1897. Geo. A. Cl'esman gets $600, born November 29, 1S74, appointed July 10, 1901. W. J. Mc-Cleary gets $600, was horn in 1868 and appointed in 1S99. Geo. Forrest gets $600, was born in 1836 and appointed in 1900, Geo. M. Biggs gets $300, was born in 1859 and appointed in 1900. John V. Horn gets $500, was born in 1866 and appointed in 1901. A. B. Stanbury, appointed 1901, gets $600 aud A. R. Cochrane, appointed 1902, gets $300. And then it follows on.
How many of these gentlemen have not passed the civil service examinations ?

None of them.
Mr. TAYLOR, Some of them are 67 years of age when they were appointed.
If they pass the civil service examination, and they are known to be good officers, we put them on the permanent list.

How can you do that when the Civil Service Act says that they Hon. Mr. PATERSON.
cannot he appointed if they are over 35 years of age.

That only refers to the inside service. It does not apply to the outside service. I think hon. members are pretty well satisfied because this was debated the other night, and, Mr. Chairman, you might as well declare the item carried and we will proceed with the next item.

This is an item in regard to which we can get some information upon another important point. The item is a very large one and there is a very general complaint that there is a large number of officers appointed in the hon. minister's department who have not passed the civil service examination. Perhaps the hon. gentleman would give us a general statement of how many officers are in Iris employ, how many have passed the civil service examination, and how many have been appointed in the last five or six years who have not passed the civil service examination.

Of course, we are dealing with what we call the outside service. The civil government estimate was passed some time ago when I gave the hon. gentleman the information lie asks now in regard to the inside service. There are 445 temporary employees throughout the Dominion and 1,172 on the permanent list. There is a total of 1,617 officers in the outside service altogether.
How many out of that number have not passed the civil service examination ?
The collectors aud subcollectors do not have to pass. None of them have passed. The inspectors do not have to pass.
Are they included in the list of 400 odd ?
The collectors are not. The temporary officers, I think as a rule, you will see, have not passed the examination.
How many are there ?
Four hundred and odd.
More than 25 per cent of the service have not missed the civil service examination.

As I said the other night, it would please me if these officers could pass the civil service examination and go on the permanent list. Temporary officers are at this disadvantage that if they are sick they do not get paid while they are absent as they do if they are on the permanent list, and they are not entitled to the three weeks holidays that the others get. Some of these officers are

just as good officers as those on the permanent list. There are men who were appointed away hack in 1880 and 1882 and from that time down. They have been in the service for from ten to fifteen years, and they are just as good officers and do the actual work of the department as well as if they had pased the civil service examination. They could have passed this examination when they came from school, but now they will not try it. I would like, speaking for myself, if parliament would pass a law that would somehow enable me to put all these men on the permanent list.

I wish to express my disapproval of that kind of procedure. If we are to have a civil service examination and the employees of the different departments are called upon to pass this examination, I think it is unfair to those who go up for examination and pass that other men who are not called upon to pass the examination are put into positions, and especially when we have a large number of men who hold the proper qualification, having passed the examination, out of employment at the present time. I think the government should either abolish the civil service examination or see to it that the men who are appointed to the different offices in the departments should have the proper qualification under the examination I have referred to.

The trouble is that a great many of these men have been employed for years. In Montreal alone there are twenty-one of these temporary employees and they were thex-e when I came into office. They are not all new appointments. We continue them and we have to continue them as 'temporary except they pass the examination. I agree with the hon. gentleman that it is desirable that they should pass if they can.
What about the future ?
We are trying to do as well as we can. We are not perfect in the direction the hon. gentleman speaks of.
Are there any of these gentlemen who have been appointed since 1897 on the temporary list who have passed the preliminary examination ?
I do not think so. We appoint them as temporary and then they pass. If a man wants to be a tide waiter or a packer he would have to pass the preliminary examination.

The only qualification the government requires now from these officials is the influence of political friends to get them in. They do not have to pass an examination now and the minister appears to be ignoring the Civil Service Act altogether. It is a dead letter in some places.
No.

It is so far as the port of Toronto is concerned. A number of men appointed there have not passed the pre-liminai'y or qualifying examinations. It is not unreasonable that this item should stand until we know the qualification of these men and their ages and all about them. What part of the $80,000 is to be spent in increasing the salaries of officers, and what officers are to have their salaries increased ? I am told that some of the men now acting as assistants and subordinates are getting as much if not more salary than the gentlemen whom they are assisting. The minister has the information at his finger ends in the department, and we should have it before we can intelligently discuss this very large item of over $1,000,000. The item had better stand until we get the information. If I had nothing else to do I could go to the Civil Service list and pick out those who are in the service of the government, but even that would not give me the temporary clerks because their names do not appear there, and there is a large percentage of them at the port of Toronto. I appeal to the Minister of Customs and to the Minister of Finance if it is not a reasonable request that this item should stand until we get this information, and get it not only with regard to Toronto but with regard to all these large ports : Montreal, Vancouver, Halifax and St. John ?

The document I was reading before gave their ages, the date of their birth and so on. I will give the hon. gentleman the officers employed in Toronto. Thomas Armstrong, acting landing waiter, $1 per week day ; A. Calder, acting messenger, $500 a year ; E. L. Darby, acting mesenger at $400 per year ; W. .1. McCleary, acting preventive officei-, $600 a year ; George Evans, acting landing waiter, at $600 per year ; George Forest, acting packer, at $1.50 per working day ; J. B. Brooks, acting packer at $500 per year; D. Fraser, acting landing waiter, $600 a year ; J. V. Horne, acting messenger, $500 per year ; J. M. Biggs, acting landing waiter season of navigation at $50 per month ; A. B. Stanbury, acting preventive officer, $600 a year ; E. H. Ross, at $20 iier month.
What does he do.
He discharges whatever duties the collector assigns him. I cannot be expected to say what they are.
It seems peculiar to have a civil servant at $20 a month.

I presume he is a boy. There is George H. Cress-man, acting preventive officer at $600 a year; A. R. Cochrane, acting preventive officer. I think that is all. I think I have given all the information that I can, and I may say that in 20 years of parliamentary life I have never heard of such explicit information being asked for or given.
Who are the temporary officers at Windsor ?
,T. W. Yearsley, J. Watson, and P. E. McEwen and the new collector, John Acheson Smith.

There are a large number of temporary officers who cannot qualify under the Civil Service Act, but who have certainly proved themselves efficient officers not only at Windsor but elsewhere. I am sure my hon. friend from North Essex who is interested in the officers around Windsor will bear me out when I say that the officers there are good officers. A great many of these officers are temporary, and it is a great injustice to them that they should be kept on the temporary list for years. It makes them subject to the influence, of both political parties and places them in an embarrassing position. The government should take some means to amend the Act so as to enable these old, tried and efficient servants to be put on the permanent list, so that they cannot be interfered with no matter what party is in power so long as they do their duty. Would the minister state what part of the $100,000 which he says he will ask for, is for the purpose of meeting the fees now paid by the transportation companies.
About $78,000 I think. That $100,000 is not in this vote, but it will, come in the supplementary estimates.
How does the minister arrive at that amount ?
The transportation companies do not pay the men direct, but the payment passes through the department, and the accountant has knowledge of it.
As I understand it, that increase is for the officers whose special duty is to accommodate the transportation companies, and it is not for the officers who are stationed along the border line.
It is for the same officers who work over hours, and that is to pay for their extra time, which we will pay in future instead of the transportation companies.
If you have officers doing day duty and night duty you need not pay them for extra time.
The men do their day duty and they earn their salary and then they are on night duty as well.
Why ?

If we had a day staff and a night staff we would have to employ extra officers, and one reason why that has not been done is that the salaries of these officers are small and they are very anxious themselves to get some Hon. Mr. PATERSON.
over time and extra pay for it. I agree with the hon. gentleman that when a man has put in 10 hours of faithful work in the day time, that ought to be enough, but they are very anxious to put in three or four extra hours to get extra pay for it and to supplement their salaries."

That was not the point 1 was making. At Fort Erie and Niagara we will say you have to have day and night officers. Having day and night officers now, how can you get in the extra time unless one officer lies off, either day or night ?
WTe do not have day and night men at these ports.

Then, that is where the department should make the change. All the trains do not come over the line in the day time. Many come at night and it is as important to have night officers as day officers. For instance, at the city of Detroit, you should have both day officers and night officers. If the hon. minister has no night officers, and if this duty is to be performed by the day officers putting in extra time, for which I presume they get a higher rate of pay than they do for day work, then the department is paying more for the service than it would pay if it had both day and night officers, and I think the department should be reorganized for that purpose.

That is what we would like to; but that item is not under discussion now; it'will come in the supplementary estimates. To have day and night men would probably be all round the best plan; but it would necessitate a larger expenditure. Suppose you have an officer to whom you are paying $600 a year, and who, for the extra time, which he is anxious to put in, makes from $150 to $200 extra. In that way he gets $750 or $800, while his salary is $600. If we were putting on a night man to do the service for which the day man is paid extra, he would expect $600 at least, the same salary as the day man. Then the day man would immediately press us and say, I was getting $S00, and you are cutting me down to $600, and I cannot live on that. We would find him pressing for as much pay for his day work alone as he had been getting for both day work and the extra work. That system would entail an extra expense upon [DOT] us, though I have no doubt it would otherwise be very satisfactory, and we may adopt it in some cases.

The hon. gentleman is referring to points where there would be only two or three hours of extra service. I am referring to points like Detroit, where it would be necessary to have men on duty all day and all night. In such cases it would cost a great deal more to pay day men extra for night services than it would to have day men and night men working the same number of hours.

As I live at the city of Windsor, I can explain perhaps how this matter has been conducted in the past at that point. In connection with the ferry company, which runs its boats up to twelve o'clock at night the customs officials get twenty-five cents an hour after six o'clock, and they are glad to get it for the extra service. The extra pay in connection with the railways amounts to $40 or $45 a month. In these ways the officers' salaries have been considerably supplemented, and they have been quite willing to meet the trains and boats at night for this extra pay. On their behalf I can say that they are opposed to this change by which the government will pay them instead of the railways. However, there has been a request for this change made by the business interests of that and other localities. While speaking on this subject, I might refer to these officials who have been in the service for many years, and yet have not been put upon the permanent list. I found in 1900, when I came in, that there were four or five men in that position. I felt that if these men, whether Conservatives or Liberals, were good officials, they should be put on the permanent list, for this reason. It appeared that when they fell ill or took their holidays, they lost their pay for the time they were absent, by not being on the permanent list. I thought that a hardship, and therefore I recommended to the hon. Minister of Customs that they should be put on the permanent list, and I think they were-two Conservatives, appointed prior to 1896, and two Liberals, appointed subsequent to that date.
How did the hon. gentleman get these officers placed on the permanent list, in view of the statement of the Minister of Customs that he regretted that he was unable to do that ?

I do not see why the civil service examination should apply so strictly to these officials as it does to other officials of the government. I thought it was nothing but right that they should be put on the permanent list, in order that they might be rescued from the disabilities I have mentioned.

That is not the question I asked. I quite concur in what the hon. gentleman says, that the evil he refers to ought to be remedied ; but I am now going to ask the Minister of Customs how the hon. member for Essex succeeded in doing what the hon. minister expressed himself as unable to do generally for officers similarly situated throughout the province. Perhaps the hon. gentleman can explain how that took place ?

I can quite understand that the rule which the hon. gentleman lays down is a good one, and that officers who have been years in the service and given satisfaction should be put on the permanent staff as preventive officers. But the hon. gentleman is constantly bringing in new men and putting them over the heads of those temporary clerks who have done efficient service for years. The hon. gentleman shakes his head, but will he say that there are no cases of new men being put over the heads of these men who have served for years as temporary clerks ? The hon. gentleman will have the support of both sides if he will bring down a Bill to cure the evils of the past and prevent them from multiplying in the future. It is no excuse for him to say that the same state of things existed in the past. If he is a progressive minister, he will put an end to it. A temporary clerk who is employed throughout the year, and who is paid practically the same as a permanent officer, should no longer be left in that position, and then no new man should be appointed to any position in the service until he has passed the qualifying examination. I should like to have an expression of opinion from the hon. gentleman on this point. We ought to know whether he is prepared to take hold of this matter courageously and deal fairly with that class of men and put an end to a condition of things which is not consistent with good service or healthy administration.
This item comprises practically the whole vote, and we cannot let it pass without more information.

The last time we had this item under discussion, some hon. gentlemen opposite said I spoke too much, and I thought that I would let them do the talking to-night. If there are to be amendments to the Act, I shall have to submit my views to my colleagues. It is only just to those older servants, who do their work well and may not be able to pass this literary examination, that they should not be compelled to pass it. As regards

future appointments, 'we are trying to do the best we can, but when deaths or other sudden changes occur we have to put a man on at once, and the way we have been doing is to appoint a man and have him pass the civil service examination later, or in some cases, where he is a valuable officer and does not feel competent to pass his examination, we put him on as a preventive officer.
I think that the previous government, either by Order in Council or in some other way, put any one who had been in the service prior to 1S82 -and down to 1896 on the permanent list, and at that time those on the permanent list came under the Superannuation Act. But, of course, the question of superannuation does not come up to-day.

Will the hon. minister have a statement prepared giving a list of the officials and the whole staff: employed in the port of Toronto and the outports connected with it, showing salary received, the dates of appointment, and the total annual expenditure ?
I have the information all here. But it would take a good while to read over this whole list of about a hundred employees.
Would the hon. minister send it over to us for a few minutes ?
It is in a book containing particulars of all the other ports as well.
W'ould not the minister have some clerk copy it 1
And bring it down on concurrence ?
Not on concurrence.
I understand the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kemp) does not want to hold the item until these particulars are furnished. The hon. gentleman wants this memorandum laid on the Table at any time.
Yes-within a day or two.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Has the hon. minister dispensed with the services of Mr. A. S. Gerald, of Prescott, and for what cause ?
He was superannuated, I think last year.
What rule does the department follow with regard to salaries paid ? Has the amount of customs receipts anything to do with it 1

Well, yes. It is not invariable. But when increases are asked the officers usually point to the increase of revenue, and, where we are able to grant increases, we like to see increased revenue if we can. That would be more particularly the case with the collector. But the payments are not uniform.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: In some ports the collectors are paid as much as those of other ports of twice the revenue.

I believe the collector at the town of Midland is paid only 8800.
I would call the minister's attention to the fact that a landing waiter was appointed, and, though the collector has been there for many years and is kept at $800, the landing waiter began with $600.

I was under the impression that we had given the collector there an increase. However, I believe we eased the work by appointing an assistant. But the port is going ahead and the revenue is $26,500. While I do not bind myself, I think the collector would be entitled to* a little more, comparing this port with others. In fact I think I have his name with others before me for consideration. I do not speak of this as making an absolute promise. This brings me to what the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) said with regard to the estimates for the several ports. We dropped that purposely. The estimates had to be made for a long distance ahead- usually a good deal over a year-It might then be found impossible to give an officer the amount that had been asked for from parliament, and the officer would say not unnaturally :	Parliament voted that money
to me. Therefore, we asked the committee to leave the matter in our hands. But I would ask hon. members of the committee if they think that injustice is done to any officer or merit is not recognized. I would take it kindly if they will mention the matter so that we may give it consideration. Of course, the committee would not wish me to go through the list of the 1,600 employees we have and give the names and salaries. But each member of the committee knows the officers in his own locality, and I shall be glad to give any information with regard to any officer asked for.

While the receipts at Midland are much larger than in many other places where the officials are paid higher salaries, this of itself does not measure the work done by the collector. For a large quantity of grain passes through that port-last year the quantity was about 15,000,000 bushels. No duty is collected on this, as it goes through in bond. I hope the minister will at least advance the collector's salary by $200. It then would only be on a par with that of many other officers who have far less to do. May I ask the minister what rent is paid for the office occupied by the collector at Midland ?
The rent is $180.

If the collector was paid at the same rate as the office is paid for, he would have $2,000 or $3,000 a year. I see that the rent was formerly only $60 a year.
.TUNE % 1903
But the leverage exerted by a warm camp follower has resulted in giving $180 for premises that would be dear at $90.

The accountant informs me that when the change of office was made we had a report from the inspector or the collector in favour of it. His recollection is, and, so far as mine extends, it is the same that the collector advised us favourably.

I think that perhaps the collector would have been afraid to report against it. There was formerly one large room, now there are two small ones. However, as a camp follower, the landlord is entitled to something, and he is satisfied with small things.

I do not know about the camp follower, but my recollection is borne out by the recollection of the accountant-and his memory of these things is pretty accurate-that when the change was made it was because of the increase of the business of the port and it may have been said that there was a vault in the new premises or something like that. At any rate our record is that the collector recommended it.
I hope the collector will be treated as liberally as the landlord.
Well, he will not be charged with being a camp follower.
What is the salary of the collector at Campbellford ?
Five hundred dollars.
Does he attend to the duties of the office himself ?

Yes,
they would be attended to by himself.
Are you sure of that ! My information is that he was an official of the Grand Trunk Railway, and some deputy was attending to the business.
Still we should hold him responsible, and more than that, he should discharge the duties himself, and for anything I know he does.
How much does the collector at Brighton get ?

Six
hundred dollars.
Is not there a much larger revenue collected at Campbellford than there is at Brighton ? I venture the assertion that there is double.

The
hon. gentleman is right.
Then how do you reconcile the two facts ?
It is difficult to reconcile them.
It is absurd to say that an officer at one port should get $500 for collecting double the revenue that an officer collects at another port who gets $600. for it.
I am afraid I am following in too large a measure what was done by my predecessors in these two places. I must do better.

I have heard that answer so often that I am sick and tired of listening to it, especially when I hear it from the Minister of Customs, whose stentorian voice I used to hear so often on this side of the House condemning the party I supported years ago. And still to-day we hear that flimsy pretext that he is following the government that he condemned. Does a business government do business in that kind of a way ? It is so absurd to my mind that I hope no intelligent minister will give that answer any more, but take the responsibility of his own acts and not say, oh, you did it. The hon. gentleman used to denounce everything the Conservative party did, and now he has-I will not say what I was going to say, but I will say that he has the impudence and the hardihood to get up and say that he is following in the steps of his predecessors that he condemned. Is it not the height of hypocrisy for a minister to follow in the footsteps of a party that he condemned ? Get out. Make footsteps of your own, and be responsible for your own footsteps, and don't lay the responsibility on a party that has long since resigned the responsibility of office, and I think very largely to the detriment of the country.

Well I have a dim recollection that I used to find some fault with the previous government. Since I have been in office I have concluded that perhaps if I knew as much then as I do now, I would not have made all the criticisms I made then. I dare say my hon. friend, if he gets my position or one like it, will come to the same conclusion. But that is no reason for continuing a bad policy. If years ago a certain salary was attached to a certain office it is a difficult thing to reduce that salary.

But he has changed the official. That argument would be good if the old official remained, but the old official at Brighton resigned, and he has appointed a new man and given him a salary very nearly as much as the old official had, while the official at Campbellford was appointed long previous, and collected an amount nearly double that was collected at Brighton. If It was the old official, there might be some argument in it, but there is no argument in it when you appoint a new man with a salary a great deal larger than

the salary of the man who is collecting a much larger revenue.

That is true, but after all you must remember that when a certain salary has been paid at a certain port, a salary which is not excessive, if you cut that salary down it is considered as degrading to the port, people look at it as lowering the standing of the town, as putting the town down.
It would not be anything derogatory to the town of Campbell-ford if you increased the salary of that official to somewhere near where it ought to be, relatively to the other man.

The hon. gentleman, I understand, has given a pledge to my hon. friend from East Toronto (Mr. Kemp), that he will bring down a detailed statement of the staff of the Toronto customs house, giving the names, ages, dates of appointment and salaries received.
Yes, I will do that.

I would like also if the hon. gentleman would bring down a statement as to what part of this $80,000 he is asking for in this year's estimates will be distributed among the officials at the port of Toronto. Of course, the hon. gentleman knows-what he is going to do, and whose salaries he is going to increase. Then 1 would like to know what plan he has adopted with reference to paying the assistant appraisers at the port of Toronto, I see some of them are getting $1,000, and some $1,600, while some of them are getting $800, some $750, some $1,200, and so on. I see the name of one very old friend of mine, Mr. McCaw, who has been there for twenty-five years, and he is getting the munificent salary of $800. Others who have not been there half as long are getting half as much more. What plan does the hon. gentleman pursue ? Does he follow the example of his predecessors in this respect, or is this a plan of his own ?
The assistant appraisers, generally speaking, are under the Civil Service Act and get from $600 to $1,500. The appraisers run from $800 to $2,000.
What cast iron rule does the hon. gentleman lay down in fixing the salaries ?

There is no cast iron rule, we try to be guided by the rules of equity and justice so far as we can. When I speak of equity and justice, it is with reference to the duties they perform. A man might be an appraiser for many years, and another man who has not been so long in the service might be getting more because he is more capable.

I hope the minister will apply the rule of equity and justice, and Mr. COCHRANE.
not merely cold justice, which I think has been the rule applied to many of these officials up to the present time. Some of these assistant appraisers are most competent men who have served many years, and their salaries remain stationary ; while others who have since come in and who are no doubt competent men, are getting half as much more, though they have not had the experience in the Customs Department, they have not had the training. Surely if equity and justice are to be the guide of the minister in apportioning the salaries to these gentlemen, there ought to be a reorganization of that department in reference to salaries, and those who have been standing stationary at a minimum salary of $750, should receive consideration. If we had the information tabulated such ns my hon. friend from East Toronto asked for, we might be able to understand the position better. The gentleman I mentioned is one of the most efficient officers in the service, and his salary is $800 ; others who have come in since are getting double.
Well, he was appointed in 1877.
A very worthy man, too.

He was seventeen or eighteen years there under my hon. friend's government, and my hon. friend must not be too hard on me for not having been able to accomplish in something over six years what the late government was not able to accomplish in eighteen years. If he was appointed at $800 he remained at that.

What accentuates this case is the fact that assistants have been brought in since then who are getting double the salary he is getting. That was not the case with the late administration. The assistants did not come in then at $1,200 or $1,800, but they came in under lower salaries. There are men who have been in the service for years getting $750 who are thoroughly competent. Surely, if the hon. minister is going to apply any rule of equity and justice, he will not allow them to stand at $750 or $S00 or $900, and bring in strangers who have not had the training or experience that these officers have had and put them at salaries at 60 or 75 per cent more than the old hands are receiving. I am sure, that, the hon. minister's attention having been drawn to these cases now, he will see that they at least get cold justice. They do not seem to have been able to get either cold or hot justice in the past.
Except there is some reason, it looks as if this officer were entitled to something more than he is getting.

There are lots of cases,
and I think the hon. minister should allow
this item to stand.
Why should it stand ?
So that we could consult with him and show him that it is all wrong.

We are asking for this extra money. We note down as far as we can before we make the estimates the officers whose salaries we think we will be able to increase. But we do not commit ourselves to it. New ports will have to come in. We have over 1,600 officers, and if I gave them $50 each of an increase the whole of this $S0,000 would be gone. I cannot do that. We have to open new ports. A case such as the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Clarke) has called attention to is a case that should receive consideration. I put it that way that it should receive consideration in case that it may not be said that I have violated my word, but lam going to look into that case. There is no use of our delaying the item, because the hon. gentleman will get the information that he desires.
It will be too late to do anything.

I have to bring down supplementaries, and there is concurrence.
Mr. 'CLARKE. We know all about concurrence; we have been there before.

The hon. minister states that the amount of revenue collected has something to do with the amount of salary paid. I would like to call his attention to the amount of revenue received in a few of the different customs houses and the salaries paid. At Bowmanville the revenue was $10,545 last year, and the salaries $1,500; Cobourg, revenue, $19,763, salaries over $3,000; Collingwood, $28,000 revenue, salaries, $1,635 ; Galt, revenue over $66,000, salaries, $1,850. This certainly seems very unfair. I have been asking the hon. minister for two years for an increase of salary for one of the officers at Galt. The amount collected is very much larger in proportion to the expenditure on salaries than at some other places.

The representations of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clare) have not been forgotten. They have been noted. I do not know if I shall be able to accomplish it, but there has been a note made of the request and it will be fully considered. Of course, Galt is an inland town. At Cobourg there is trains-shipping and there are outports under the collector.
There are outports of Galt, too.
I suppose there are.

When you take into consideration how much more is collected at Galt
than at the towns I have cited, it is hard to understand why there should not be some increase if there is any fair division of salaries.
Would the hon. gentleman turn to page F-11 of the Auditor General's Report and explain what he means by ' acting collector D. Ferguson ' and ' acting landing waiter T. Morse ' ?
At St. Thomas 7
Yes.

It means that these officers are not appointed by Order in Council at once. When they are not appointed by Order in Council at once they are referred to as acting collectors or landing waiters. When they are put on the permanent list by Order in Council they will appear as ' collector ' or ' landing waiter.' The term ' acting collector ' just shows that when he was first appointed he was not appointed by Order in Council.
Has the Order in Council been passed making Mr. Ferguson the permanent collector 7
Yes, he was appointed permanently on May 20 last.
What about Mr. Morse 7
Mr. Morse was appointed permanently on April 1 last.

Mr. Chairman, before leaving this item, I desire to remind the hon. minister of the promise he made last year in regard to the superannuation of James Curry, the late collector of customs at Charlottetown. Mr. Curry was superannuated at the age of sixty-seven years, an active and vigorous man. I have here 'Hansard' of last year :

I did not expect to be asked for the details and hare not got the information here, hut I will bring it to the hon. gentleman.

I would like to ask the hon. minister the salary that is paid to the custom-house officer at Napanee and the salary of the landing waiter there ? I think the customs officer there is also the inspector of excise.

I could not tell the hon. gentleman about that.
I would like to have that information.
Would the hon. gentleman make that request when the inland revenue items are under consideration ?

There ought to be enough members of the government present to give such information when it is asked for. There is no reason why there should only be two or three members of the government in the House. I do not see why they should not sit here as well as the rest of us.

Of course, the miniser whose estimates are under consideration has to assume the responsibility of explaining them, and some of the other ministers can be spared to attend to other pressing duties. This gentleman is also an officer of the Inland Revenue, and when the Minister of Inland Revenue is asking for his vote he will explain about him.
What is his salary as landing waiter ?

And you do not know
what he is getting as an inland revenue officer ?

I will try and be here when the inland revenue estimates are up.
What number of officers were appointed in the Customs Department last year who did not pass the civil service examination, and what number were appointed in that department altogether ?
I cannot give that information to-night, as I did not know it would be asked for, but I shall get it.

Will the minister also give us a list of the appointees this year who have passed the examination ? And now that the attention of the minister has been called to the anomaly of some assistant appraisers receiving $750 a year and some $1,600, I think he should give some explanation.
A note has been made of that, and it will be considered.

You cannot assume that because they are all called preventive officers they discharge the same duties, because some of them are in the long room receiving entries, which is the most particular work, while others of them may be merely out on the wharf.

speechtext:
Guelph collects $113,000 and-gets $3,550. In Toronto it costs $87,000 to collect $6,000,000, and in Montreal it costs $155,000 to collect $10,000,000. There is no comparison there.
The MINISTER OB'1 CUSTOMS. No, they vary very much.

I wish to ask the Minister of Customs if it is the intention to adopt any more stringent rules or regulations to prevent the customs revenue from being defrauded by continental goods being admitted as British goods, and getting the benefit of the British preferential tariff ?

We want to do all we can in that way. I do not know that we can devise anything better than we have at present. If there is any practicable way in which they can be strengthened, wet would be glad to be informed of it. I think we have done about all we can do by means of rules and regulations. As to carrying them out, we are insisting on our officers being as vigilant as possible.

But there is no barrier against certain classes of goods which are made on the continent coming here from Great Britain as if they were British manufactures. The certificate which the government requires to be on the invoice, and which is signed by the shipper or the clerk of the shipper, is no barrier. That is all that the government does In reference to this matter. When the preferential tariff was first adopted, a declaration was suggested, and a! form was given to the collectors of customs which made it compulsory for shippers to go before a notary public, a commissioner, a municipal officer of a city or town, a British consul, or a secretary or a president of a chamber of commerce, and take an oath. That was in 1897 ; but in 1898 the government saw fit to put into effect a different sort of obligation-an ordinary certificate. That certificate can be made by a senior or junior clerk in the employ of the exporting firm, and it is merely the ordinary form of declaration. The hon. Minister of Customs knows, from his experience as a business man, of what little importance these certificates are in the eyes of exporters or shippers. We
all know what little importance some shippers place upon an affidavit, and they place far less importance upon the mere signing of an invoice. This form in use at the present time, I know ' from personal experience, is often signed by a clerk employed by a firm which has probably a hundred invoices a day going out. The form going to Canada may be different from that going to India or Australia ; and that is the only barrier that the Customs Department has. provided against continental goods coming into Canada and obtaining the preference as British goods. I believe it has been the intention of the government not to allow that to go on. In 1901, I remember the hon. Minister of Finance stating in the House that that was not the intention of the government, and he said practically what the hon. Minister of Customs says now, that if any other device could be suggested, lie would be pleased to hear it. I am informed by one of our leading wholesale dry goods merchants of Toronto, a man who has had great experience in importing, that he could not say of certain classes of goods whether they were of German or Belgian or English manufacture. This gentleman stated this case to me : ' Some years ago I bought from a firm of very high standing in Bradford, before the preferential tariff came in-tol effect, a certain class of dress goods as being of British manufacture, and they were placed in my warehouse in Toronto. My son was at the time living and undergoing an apprenticeship in a town in France. A short time afterwards he came to Toronto on a visit, and saw these goods in my warehouse, and asked where I had got them. I said from Priestley, of Bradford. M.v son said that they had been made in the factory in France where he was employed.' This same gentleman told me that he would not be prepared to swear in what country the following goods were manufactured : dress goods, certain classes of laces, silks, ribbons, velvets, velveteens, hosiery, underwear, gloves, buttons, linens, printed goods, and flannels. These different classes of goods, I believe, are" coming into this country all the time as being of Rritish manufacture, and I believe that a very large proportion of them are largely German goods. A short time ago there appeared in the Toronto ' News ' an article headed ' How some German firms avoid paying full duty. Many manufacturers send goods to Canada via England. They thus save ten per cent. Germany to Canada, thirty-five per cent ; England to Canada, twenty-five per cent ; Germany to England, free.' The article, of which I wili just read a small portion goes on to say :
The Canadian tariff on manufactured woollen goods imported from Germany is 35 per cent compared with 25 per cent imposed on British manufactures of the same class entering Canada. As these German goods are admitted free into England, the German manufacturer at once sees that by sending his goods to Canada via
*

England, he saves 10 per cent in duties. Walter Muhlinghaus, Toronto, who represents the Hermann Muhlinghaus Company, Lennep, Germany, states that this unfair and round-ahout method of getting into the Canadian market is resorted to by several firms. With this end in view they established agencies in London and sold their goods 'through that medium. Mr. Muhlinghaus states, however, that his father's firm, to which he is attached, sends their manufactures direct from Germany to Canada.
Frequently this German agency was placed with a British manufacturer, who availed himself of what was known as the ' business secret,' that is he sold these German goods as the ' made in England ' article, and in most cases the Canadian purchaser was none the wiser. The classes of goods in question were underwear and similar clothing.
Owing to the comparative cheapness of production in Germany, the British manufacturer found that he could buy certain lines of German goods and sell them in Canada at greater profit than by manufacturing the goods in England. Mr. Muhlinghaus stating that the cost of production was at least 30 per cent cheaper in Germany than in England.
I have satisfied myself that what I am stating is correct, and I believe the officers of the Customs Department know that this kind of thing is going on, and I have no doubt the hon. Minister of Customs knows it. It is a difficulty which should be overcome in some way or other. The British preference was not given for the purpose of letting in continental goods under it and thus swindling the government. There is another point I would submit. Under that German surtax, I believe there is a new regulation, but it does not amount to anything more than the old one. The temptation to get in German goods from Great Britain will be greater than it was heretofore. There is absolutely nothing in the way except a mere certificate of the exporter or his clerk on the bottom of the invoice, which means nothing. The buyer on this side does not consider that it is his duty to investigate. He sees his neighbour doing the same thing and it will not do for him to suggest to the Customs Department that the goods may be German, Belgian, Austrian or French. He says to himself : ' My neighbour will not do that, why should I ? If I do it, it will result in raising the duty on myself.' That sort of injustice is being perpetrated and these foreign goods are coming in as British. Under this German surtax the temptation will be greater, the swindle will be greater, and the government should devise some better method of dealing with the case.
How is it that the customs officers will not give receipts for customs duties paid at the various ports of entry-a straight receipt to the importer or his broker ?
It has not been considered necessary. The importer pays his duty and gets his goods.

When an importer sends money to his broker, the broker Mr. KEMP.
pays the duty at the port of entry and the importer has no check on his broker.
If the merchant gives the broker his check, it comes back to him through the bank. If he remitted the cash, he would have to trust his broker.

But he wants to know the items for which this money was spent. I do not see any valid reason why the officer should not give a receipt. This is done on the other side, right across the river, and it would be a great convenience to importers. The custom is to receipt a third copy of the entry, but that is a cumbersome way and it takes just as long as it would to give a straight receipt.

When persons are on the ears with small parcels, the officer gives them a receipt, but it is not usual in ordinary transactions, and this is the first time I have heard any complaint on that score. As a rule the brokers are responsible men and the merchant knows with whom he is dealing.

It is not a matter of very great importance, but I know that a great many complaints have been made. I know of cases where the parties absolutely refused to pay the duty unless they got a receipt, and I can not see any reason why one should not be given. A proper form might be made out and submitted to the customs officers for approval.
I would like to have an explanation with regard to the matter I brought up.

I really cannot give any more information than I have already given. As the hon. gentleman has rightly stated, the department do not intend to let goods in, under the preference, that are not entitled to it. A certificate is required from the exporter, signed by himself or signed by one of bis clerks, who must declare that be has personal knowledge of what he certifies to. But whether signed by the clerk or the merchant, the house is held just as firmly. The hon. gentleman is right in saying that *when the preference was first introduced we required an affidavit accompanying the invoice. But we found that a source of great anuoyance to our imiJorters. Houses in the old country complained very much. They complained that they had to pay a fee of fifteen cents for each certificate, and in some cases they had to get their certificates from the Chamber of Commerce, and there was a good deal of trouble and annoyance especially in the eases of small parcels. The department concluded that if a house would deliberately sign a declaration on the invoice in the name of the firm, which was not true, they would also make a false affidavit. As far as the penalties

are concerned, these penalties would follow just as surely a false declaration as a false affidavit. We thought that it would ease the trade in the old country and please the importers here and be just as safe to the revenue to have a declaration instead of an affidavit. You may say that a man might sign a declaration who would hesitate to make an affidavit, but I do not think there would be many cases of that kind. If a man would be careless in signing a declaration, he would be equally careless in the matter of an affidavit. We may probably be able to do a little better in the future in the way of supervision in the old country, because my hon. colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, is appointing commercial agents in some of the cities in the old country. One has been lately appointed in Birmingham, and if we have any doubts about imports of hardware from there, we can avail ourselves of the services of that commercial agent. WTe are giving the matter every attention and care, and I will hail with pleasure any suggestion that would be workable and supplement the present regulations.

I did not know that there was a fee charged by the secretary or president of the Chamber of Commerce, but if there was, it could have been but a very small fee. I happened to be in London about the time this order was changed, and Mr. Murray, the [DOT] secretary of the London Chamber of Commerce drew my attention to it and prophesied that the result would be very unsatisfactory. His reason was that in London particularly, there are all kinds of merchants, and because a firm in this country imports from a certain firm in London, it does not necessarily follow that the firm in London is composed of British subjects of the high character of British merchants, whom we were glad always to think of as men of great integrity. These men are foreigners, to a very large extent. They reside in England sometimes only for a short time ; they are people of all nationalities, and if the precaution were taken by the government of insisting on their going before a notary or a secretary or a president of a chamber of commerce, and making an affidavit, that would be- a greater safety for the government and for the revenue than the mere declaration now required.
1 think the government will do well to reconsider the step it took in 1898 in framing the new regulations, especially in view of the German surtax. The temptation will be greater under that even than it was before.
I repeat that I do not think that the certificate at the bottom of the invoice amounts to anything in at least three-quarters of the cases. In the other 25 per cent it might be of some value. But, on the whole, it is no effective guard against bringing in continental goods and passing them through as British goods.
In fact it is not worth a continental.

I cannot agree that it is no guard. With regard to Mr. Murray himself, I imagine that the fee on account of these affidavits was a persona] perquisite. I take it that these fees would not go into the coffers of that chamber of commerce but would be one of the perquisites of his office.
I do not know what the charge was.

If what I suppose is true, he would naturally favour having that continued. But there is this value to the declaration made by the firm that if there is a flaw, we seize the goods, and the importer, as an innocent party would have this recourse against the exporter, that, under our customs law, the perpetrator of the fraud could not collect for the goods sent to this country. They run the risk of having their goods forfeited and not being able to collect them. While some houses might be lacking in principle, the fear of the power of the law is there to help to keep them straight.

May I ask the minister what steps he takes or can take, if there is a fraud in the matter ? How, in the name of conscience, will he or his officers find out that there has been a fraud ? Will he enlighten us on that point ? We have drawn the attention of the minister to this question in years past, but he has never enlightened us on the subject. Will he do so now ?
The party who signs that declaration knows whether it is a fraud or not.
Yes, but how can the minister's officers find out if it is a fraud or not ?

By their expert knowledge, they might be able in a ease of a certain article to know whether it is an article of German manufacture or not. In the case of a textile, I judge, that would be a difficult matter. My hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Brock) would be able to tell us about that.

But the difficulty is made greater by the fact that raw material from which the goods are made may be German. They may be manufactured in Germany and yet come in under the so-called British preference. How can there be the slightest safeguard, under the present system, against goods brought in under affidavit, that they are British goods, and yet, without a farthing of British labour put up on them ? The handicraft is the same. How, then, can the hon. minister's officers detect any difference ?

392*

We have to rely very largely upon the affidavit. But if we are going to have a preference that difficulty occurs and you cannot help it. Has there been any deficiency on our part-that is the practical thing.
The whole preference is deficient.

The hon. gentleman's argument is against the preference as a whole; but we have it, and we have to deal with it. The question is now, are we lacking in anything that would enable us to exercise greater circumspection 7

But the hon. minister is making the whole thing impracticable. The regulation cannot be practicably carried out. He says this is a British preference and we contend that it is a German preference. The government should change the name of it and call it a continental preference, not a British preference. The hon. gentleman cannot tell us any way by which he can find out where the goods are produced, unless he watches their manufacture from the time they are begun until the time they are exported to Canada. That has always been our contention, and now the hon. gentleman admits that it is right. Well, what does he intend to do under the circumstances 7 Does he intend to allow these goods to come in as British goods under the preference when he admits that he cannot know, without watching the goods in the course of manufacture, whether the affidavit on the invoice is right or not 7 Is he not going to advise his colleagues that this whole thing is a fraud on the face of it 7 It is surely wrong to call this a British preference when he himself admits that foreign goods are coming in here and getting the advantage of the preference. The German manufacturer and the middleman in England and in New York are the only persons who are profiting by the preference-not the British artisan or manufacturer.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) is mistaken. Of course he is leading the discussion away from what is really my point, the point that I seek to defend. He is opening up the question of the policy of the government.
For the reason that the hon. gentleman admits that there is practically no safeguard.

No, I do not admit that. I think we have a great safeguard in the declaration, and another in the expert knowledge of our officers. I hope we shall have an additional safeguard in our commercial agents. The hon. gentleman's argument is against the whole preference. The goods, to come in, must be declared to have been finished in Great Britain. We require the finishing process there.

There must be at least twenty-five per cent of the value of the goods of British production, and this twenty-five per cent must include the last stage of manufacture. They could not send out British goods which would make twenty-five per cent of the completed product and have them manufactured in Germany and sent here. The last process must be in Great Britain. The hon. gentleman asks what further we can do 7 Well, for instance, our attention was called to linseed oil which was coming in under the preference. We were informed that it was made largely from Argentine seed. This raised a very nice question. If the material was pressed from Argentine seed it could not come in under the preference. But if the seed came from India or some other British possession entitled to the preference, the value of the seed would be counted in towards the twenty-five per cent. We wrote to the High Commissioner and he investigated at the'headquarters of the manufacturer, what proportion of Argentine seed went into the production of the oil. We take all the steps we can to guard the revenue. As to saying that you can absolutely determine all these points, I am free to admit that that cannot be done. But do not blame the customs department for that. We have to carry out the law. The hon. gentlemen about me, forming the parliament of Canada, have, said :	We want this preference. Parliament having declared that these goods shall come in under the preference we cannot exclude them. We let them come in under what seem to us the best regulations. But, if there has been a fraud, we seize the goods and the man who has made the false declaration cannot collect for them.

How many seizures have been made, because of false declaration, of goods brought in under the British preference 7 Has there been one 7 Surely that is an easy question for the minister and not an unreasonable one. The preference has been in force since August, 1891, I believe I hope it will not tax the memory of the minister too much to tell us, how many seizures have been made because of false declarations since that time.
No, 1 cannot tell the hon. gentleman. I do not think there have been many.
Was there one 7
I should think so.
More than one 7
I think so. We had a good many seizures.

I am asking about the seizures because of false declarations under the British preference. If there was only one, the hon. gentleman could give us some particulars, because it would be im-

pressed upon his memory. Where was that seizure made ?
It is not impressed upon my memory particularly.
If the minister will bring down the information
I could not tell offhand.
Bring us down the memorandum when we next discuss the hon. gentleman's estimates, showing how many of these seizures there have been, where, and the amounts involved.
The department does not give the names.
Only the place, and the amounts involved.
You are asking me to bring down so many things I am afraid I shall forget some.

I am very sorry to burden the minister. But how can he know, except from the declarations, whether 25 per cent of British labour has been added to the value of these goods ? I need not remind the hon. gentleman that the circular issued by his department to the collectors- in 1897 permitted the goods to come in as having had 25 per cent of value added to them, if the person who bought them in Germany, or Belgium, or France or Switzerland, sold them for export to Canada at 25 per ceut more than he paid for them ini the foreign country. That 25 per cent was to be accounted, according to the instructions issued by the hon. gentleman's own officials, as British labour, as an increased value given to the goods by British labour. In interpreting exactly what the hon. gentlman meant, how can he state that these goods have been enhanced by British labour to the value of 25 per cent ? Our contention has been that it is not necessary to add even one per cent to the value of these goods by British labour, foreign goods can and do come in under the preference. That is the reason why we protest against the so-called British preference, because we claimed it was a continental preference. Will the minister explain how his departmental officers could tell that 25 per cent had been added by British labour ?

But that is 25 per cent on.
Mr. CLARKE, If the merchant in England or the middleman in England purchased $800 worth of goods made in Germany and sold them to the Canadian importer at $1,000, thus adding 25 per cent, the difference
between what he paid for them and what he sold them for was to be counted, under the instructions issued by the hon. gentleman, as British labour. That is the point.

They have to be enhanced in value 25 per cent, enhancing in value 25 per cent means that 33i per cent has been added, because 25 per cent off is equal to 33J per cent on. Now there is no profit at 33J per cent on a wholesale transaction.
25 per cent includes the difference, the addition, made to the goods purchased on the continent, when they land in England and are sold in Canada, and may embrace insurances, freight, boxes, &c.

Here is $1 worth of goods, if they come in there must be additional value given to them as British labour. Take that 25 per cent off and that leaves 75 cents, 25 on 75 is 33J advance. NoV there is no 33^ profit made by the wholesale merchants, or anything of that kind. I think in textiles the cost of the labour averages about 331 per cent. So while 25 per cent of the finished value of the goods is required to be put on, it is about 331 advance.

I say that if the British merchant or the middleman brings in $800 worth of goods from the continent and sells them for $1,000 to a Canadian merchant, he has added 25 per cent to their value according to the instructions issued by the hon. gentleman, and he gets the advantage of the preference, although British labour has not added one cent to their value.
That would be a simple and direct fraud.
That is what we claim.
And we claim that this fraud is permitted by the department because of the circular of instructions issued in 1897.

Can the hon. gentleman point out any other way by which a fraud like that can be avoided ?
Mi'. CLARKE. We ai'e asking the hon. gentleman to do that.

But hon. gentlemen are finding fault, and I think it is not unreasonable to say, after we tell how we are doing it, that they should suggest any better way if they are able. One suggestion he has given that there should be an affidavit instead of a declaration. We tried that, and we abandoned it. But what other plan can he suggest ? The argument of the hon. gentleman is against the preference altogether. That does not concern our duty. The duty of the department is to administer the law as parliament, including hon. gentlemen opposite, have enacted. Parliament said, we want a British preference, we want the goods to come into this country

that are made iu Britain at a lower rate than those that are made in other countries. That being the law, we hare to administer it, and in doing that we try to keep foreign nations from taking advantage of that preference illegally. I furnished the hon. gentleman with all the1 declarations, rules and regulations, and X think we have done all we can without unduly hampering the trade. But I shall be obliged to hon. gentlemen if they will tell us of any other step we can take that we have not taken.

The minister has at last taken our advice very kindly, and he has put on the surtax. They were slow to take advice offered from this side of the House, but at length they did it. But let me read for the hon. gentleman's information one paragraph contained in the circular issued by his department in 1897, which will sustain our contention :
In estimating the labour of the United Kingdom entering into the production of articles manufactured therein partly from imported material, the extent of such labour may he reckoned by the value of the manufactured article ready for shipment at the place of production after deducting therefrom the value on entering within the limits of the United Kingdom, represented by the component parts of such articles which are the produce of countries not entitled to the benefits of the preferential tariff.
Surely that can only have one meaning, that if the goods are sold for export to Canada for 25 per cent over and above what they cost when imported into England from the| continent, the difference between what they cost and what they are sold for is to be acounted as British labour, although there has not been necessarily one per cent of British labour or any other kind of labour added to them.
The hon. gentleman has the latest circular that we issued, I gave it to him the other day. There is one-quarter to be added to the value of the goods.
No ; the hon. gentleman must not persist in maintaining that after this circular has been read.

There is the declaration that they have to make. It enters into not less than one-quarter of the value of the article. If the article is of German origin, there must be 25 per cent of it that is the result of British labour. Take that off and the valuation is 75 cents. Twenty-five per cent on 75 per cent will not make up a dollar, but 33J per cent will, and therefore there is an enhancement in value of literally 33J per cent. I have not that circular.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: There is no difference between that circular and the one which my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) has read. If an exporter in England purchases goods in Germany and makes 25 per cent profit on the transaction, he can take that declaration, because that 25 per cent is put on by his labour in purchasing and selling again. It comes down to the bald fact that 25 per cent of the value of the article so exported has not been added by goods of British origin going into it or British labour being employed in its manufacture. But it may be increased 25 per cent in value by the party who has purchased it in Germany, imported it and sold it again. He can take that declaration, and it is being done every day. The country is being flooded with German goods and they have the benefit of this preference, although they have not been enhanced in value by material or labour in England, except the value that is represented by wrapping and stamping.

The hon. minister has given us the form of declaration that exporters have to subscribe to, and he accompanies that with an explanation as to how they estimate the increased value. That circular provides that if the value Is enhanced by 25 per cent over what the article cost the exporter in a foreign country that fact will be sufficient to justify him in making that declaration.

The hon. minister has a very ingenious argument in regard to 25 per cent off being equal to 33J per cent on, but I guarantee that not one exporter in a thou-

sand understands the matter in that way. He understands it in the way that the hon. member for West Toronto understood it when he said that if $800 was the value of goods (purchased in Germany and they were sold for $1,000 in this country, the $200 difference would be considered the 25 per cent. At any rate, if the goods were worth $800, the exporter in Great Britain might calculate his profit to be a certain amount, the carriage of these goods to be a certain amount, the packing to be a certain amount, and it might result in there not being 1 per cent of British labour put upon them under the regulations which are in effect in the Customs Department of this country. I think the argument of the hon. minister shows that he admits that fraud is perpetrated. I do not think he is prepared to deny that fraud is being perpetrated, that the regulations do not cover the situation and do not prevent continental goods coming in here and getting the benefit of the preference. The quantity that comes in, it is impossible to state. It is an indefinite quantity. The hon. minister says to us, having admitted that fraud does exist, and having admitted the correctness of our argument : What would you do ? I ask the hon. minister if it is the duty of this side of the House to prescribe what should be done? Whose invention is this Is it not the invention of the government, and should it not be their duty to invent some means to overcome the difficulty to which we have referred ?

Quite so, but I know if the hon. gentleman knew anything more that could be done to prevent possible fraud-mind, I only admit possible fraud ; I do not say that fraud is committed, as I do not think there are many frauds committed-but I believe that if the hon. gentleman knew of any step that could be taken that would tend to greater security, his sense of patriotism, his desire to see the law enforced, would impel him voluntarily to give me his suggestion. These hon. gentlemen have not suggested anything. Although we are doing the best we can, they believe the best we can do is ineffectual. I grant that possibly it may be, but I do not know of any better system. When I was in England last year accompanied by my secretary, when we got through our work, we met a great many merchants. We were waited upon by a large commercial body in the hotel one day for the purpose of discussing an insolvency law. The delegation was composed of large shippers. I availed myself of the opportunity of finding out if they thought there were any large frauds perpetrated in reference to the preferential tariff. These were shippers of high standing and men whose word you would not doubt at all. Their interest would be, if any fraud was being perpetrated by any other house, to reveal it to me, because if any other house was perpetrating a fraud
of this kind it would beat them out in the Canadian trade. Notwithstanding that their interest was to reveal any fraud if it existed, their reply was that they were not aware of a fraud of that kind being committed, and they did not think it was being committed to any extent. We had other opportunities of procuring information in regard to the subject, and my secretary, who is fairly up in the department, visited the establishments of some of the houses interested in the Canadian trade, and he was unable to discover that fraud existed to any extent.

These great shippers and leading merchants were supplied with the circular that provided that the profit of the middleman was to be counted as British labour. There was no fraud as far as they were concerned in interpreting the circular which the hon. gentleman had issued.
There is no such profit as 33J per cent on the whole transaction. There is nothing of that kind.

If our contention is right these gentlemen with whom the minister and
his secretary came in contact could not say that a fraud was committed, except it be a huge fraud on the Canadian public ?n calling the preference a British preference, when as a matter of fact goods that had not one dollar of British labour in them were classed as British.

Their testim#ny was in a general way that they did not believe that fraud was perpetrated under this preference tariff. We made personal inquiries and in some cases we availed of the services of the officers of the High Commissioner. I hope I may be permitted to say that this is outside of my estimates, which is a vote to pay the officers who must be paid, and I think you might now conclude to give me the money provided I spend it in a proper manner, which I will try to do.
It is pertinent to the estimate that we should ask for the number of seizures because of fraud. I understand the minister will bring that down ?
I might not be able to trace that for a number of years.
For the last two or three years.

The linseed'oil manufacturers of Canada sent a deputation to wait on the minister to complain that foreign oil was being imported under the name of the British preference. My recollection is that we took steps to get the facts from the people who manufacture this oil, and the information we got from them

did not agree with the information given us by our friends here. It was very clear to nie that the labour in pressing the oil itself did not amount to 25 per cent, but if a certain quantity of seed coming from a country entitled to the preference entered into that oil, that together with the cost of production would entitle it to enter. My recollection is that while they claim that they use some of the Argentine" flax, that there was enough of the other kind to bring it under the preference, while our manufacturers here claim that while they ran the Argentine seed they ran it pure, and they do not accept the statement that it is mixed. These manufacturers told us that to mix the two would lessen the value and that it was against their interest to do so. We were not able to determine whether it was right or wrong, and I have not heard very much since from my linseed oil friends or whether they fe.el that they are not getting fair play. It is one of the most difficult questions we had to tackle.

I would like to know from the minister if there is any way of ascertaining whether there is any other seed than this Argentine seed in this linseed oil ? I suppose the minister admits that there is hot 25 per cent of British labour in the manufacture of this oil ?
Yes.
They got over that by saying that there was some British seed in it, and the minister let it go at that.

We had inquiries instituted, and my recollection is- I speak subject to correction-that they claimed there was enough of Indian seed going into the oil so that with the cost of production it brought it within the preference.
Could you tell from the oil itself whether there was Calcutta seed in it or not.
I cannot, and I do not know whether our experts could. Can my kon. friend (Mr. McGowan) tell ?
No.
Well, if you cannot tell I do not suppose that our experts can. It is a difficult matter, but we took all the steps we could.

I do not know anything about these other things which my hon. friend from Toronto speaks of, but I am perfectly satisfied that in the matter of linseed oil the revenue of the country is being defrauded in connection with this preference. The minister says that there is not 25 per cent of British labour in the manufacture of this oil and that there must be enough British-grown seed to make up for the deficiency of the labour. I can tejl the minister that this is not so. There is not Hon. Mr. PATERSON.
25 per cent British labour, and every one knows that there is no Calcutta seed going into it. I think the department should take the trouble to ascertain whether they are being defrauded or not in this matter.
The British colonies are entitled to the preference and British seed grown in India gets the benefit of it.
How do you know that there is Calcutta seed in it ?
If there is not it is not entitled to the preference.
It comes in all the same.

The labour expended in producing this seed is as much entitled to count in the preference as the labour of crushing it in England. The contention is that the cost of producing the seed together with the labour of crushing it in England entitles it to the preference.
Did they furnish any information as to the portion of Calcutta seed in that oil ?
I think so.
Then I would like to have that evidence brought down.

If the hon. gentleman 'would not consider it too much trouble to come to my office, I will be glad to show him the efforts we made in order to arrive at a decision in this matter. I know that the views of the men here who understand the business do not agree with the views we received from the English producers.
We are to understand that the information furnished by the linseed oil manufacturers of Canada was found to be incorrect.
Well, it would be better to say that the department has not come to a decision yet.

The minister has been asking for suggestions to overcome this difficulty, and I wish to remind him that the linseed oil manufacturers of Canada gave him some very valuable suggestions on that score. I will just read one clause :
Air. Paterson then asked us what we could propose. We suggested that all persons making such a declaration should make a detailed statement of where the materials were obtained from which the goods were produced.
That is to say, you would alter your declaration so that the party who made the linseed oil would be compelled to make a declaration stating where the seed came from out of which the oil was made in England before it came to this country. May I ask the minister if he proposes to take action

and adopt the suggestion of the linseed oil manufacturers, which I am satisfied would keep out of this country the foreign article ?
that there may be some come in. 1 admit the possibility, but I do not go further than that.
That is worth considering.

The hon. minister would have to go further. If a portion came from a British colony which was entitled to the preference, he would want the declaration to state the proportion coming from the colony and the proportion coming from a foreign country.

It would appear, from the discussion that has taken place to-night, that the charges or statements made on a great many occasions with reference to the importation of goods from Germany, France and other foreign countries into this country, under the British preference were true. The Minister of Customs practically admits that they are true.
I say there might be some come in.

That being the case, what steps have the government of Canada taken to protect the revenue ? So far as I know, they rely on the certificate, which has not the force of a declaration, and that in the face of the fact that the department knows from past experience that certain foreign houses in Great Britain have been in the habit of defrauding the revenue continuously. Not many years ago, under the present Minister of Customs, a foreign house in Montreal was detected in a very extensive undervaluation of invoices, carried on for a number of years, in which it was perfectly clear that any statement or declaration made by a house of that character would be perfectly worthless ; and yet, from the statement made to-night by "the lion. Minister of Customs, he has relied entirely on evidence in the form of declarations or statements of people of that character of those with whom he had that experience in the past. Virtually the understanding at which the House must arrive, after hearing the minister's statement, is that in this matter the country and the revenue of the country are absolutely unprotected. There are a great many articles of foreign manufacture, which it has been asserted from time to time have been getting the benefit of the British preference, including some goods to which it was scarcely conceivable that any value could he added after their production ; for instance, cutlery, crockery, certain classes of textile fabrics, silks, neckwear, hats and caps, and many other classes of goods. I did
not say that. I admit that it is possible1

person engaged in these fraudulent transactions. Nothing whatever would appear to have been done to secure detection or conviction. If I did not misunderstand the hon. minister to-night, he has practically admitted that he knows that a certain proportion of customs entries are fraudulent.
