I understood that a portion of the machinery of his department was the employment of men thoroughly versed in the manufacture of the several branches in which undervaluation is practiced, and I am surprised to find that while the hon. minister was apparently compelled to admit that all the statements made with reference to the evasion of the preferential clause are correct, and so far he has taken no means to secure the detection of the guilty parties and prevent the continuance of those frauds. The country would sustain him in any reasonable expenditure in order to protect our manufacturers and the honest merchants by seeing that the preference we have given so generously to the mother country should not be taken advantage of by foreigners. If the hon. gentleman would apply the same energy to the prevention of frauds on the revenue by this abuse of the preferential clause which he does to putting down the operation of smugglers throughout our sea-coast, he would find that this House would cordially second his efforts. There can be nothing more unsatisfactory than to find that the preference which Canada has given the mother country is not being enjoyed by the merchants of the mother country at all, but by foreigners, to whom certainly we would not be Willing to extend any favour whatever, particularly at the expense of the manufacturers and the workingmen of Canada. It is quite possible that the hon. minister may not care to take the House into his confidence. He may possibly have taken some steps in this direction and not care to disclose them, in case that might prevent there being successful. Well, if he is in a position to say that he is prevented by the fear of publicity from fully taking the House into his confidence, I would not be disposed to press him unduly, but the impression I gathered from the whole discussion leads me to the belief that the minister was of the opinion that we were being cheated, but could look upon it with a good natured smile as one of those things no fellow could understand. It was a sort of fourteen-fifteen puzzle, which he was inclined to pass over to this side of the House in order that we might see what we could do with it. That certainly is the impression which the hon. gentleman left on my mind. This energetic minister of an energetic government practically confessed that he was beaten and threw up the sponge. He practically admitted that if these foreign houses in Britain choose to continue to send us goods Mr. BELL.
of those different classes under the preferential clause, he did not see what he could do and was disposed to ask what we thought should be done. Does the hon. gentleman wish us to understand that there are insuperable difficulties in connection with this preference, that he has exhausted his ingenuity, that the cleverest minds in his department are powerless to devise a remedy, and that he is absolutely at loss to know what to do ? Is that the position the hon. gentleman takes ?
No.

I am very glad to hear him say so, but might I ask him to take us to some extent into his confidence and tell us what he proposes to do. It is not at all satisfactory for the people of Canada to feel that they are being defrauded by foreigners, who are ingenious enough to get the advantage of the preferential clause, which it was never intended should apply to them. The people of Canada will not long tolerate a minister at the head of the Department of Customs who admits that he cannot remedy this condition of affairs, and it seems to me that it ought not to be very difficult to devise some means of assuring the conviction of those who thus evade our customs laws. There are only a very few business centres from which these suspicious invoices may come, and but a small number of houses which do this kind of business; is there any insuperable difficulty in watching the operations of those houses ? Can the government not secure evidence, if necessary, by acquiring information from the employees of these houses ? Convictions could thus be secured and the minister could make up a black list of exporters of the mother country, houses dealing in the class of goods under suspicion no statement from which would be accepted in any custom house under the control of the hon. gentleman.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bell) is mistaken when he says that the hon. Minister of Customs has admitted that all the statements made with regard to fraudulent invoices under which German or other continental goods obtain the benefit of the British preference are correct. The hon. gentleman's (Mr. Bell) whole speech was based upon the assumption that the hon. Minister of Customs had admitted these statements. But the hon. minister has not admitted anything of the sort. What he said was-the hon. gentleman will no doubt reccollect it when I remind him of it-that it was possible that fraudulent invoices had been sent and goods fraudulently entered. Wherever you have a system of taxation somebody will manage to evade some portion of his just due. The difficulty is all the greater and the temptation is greater if you have two rates of duty on articles precisely the same or of a similar character. But I wish to say that I think

it is a mistake to have the discussion proceed upon the assumption that there is widespread fraud in this matter. I have not the same information on this subject as my hon. friend the Minister of Customs. But to'the extent of my information I agree with him in saying that I do not believe that such frauds exist to any considerable extent. And I will tell why. The Minister of Customs has said that he appealed to reputable business houses in Great Britain on the subject-and they would have an interest in seeing to it that fraudulent dealers were not permitted to carry on their business in this way-and the best information he could obtain was that this fraud was not likely to be perpetrated to any great extent. Among the numerous gentlemen who have waited on me with regard to tariff matters were many who believed that German goods were being fraudulently brought in as British. But I think I do not go too far when I say that ih most cases when they were asked to look into the matter carefully and see if they could fortify their impression-because it was only an impression-by reference to particular cases, they failed to do so. We did not ask them to give public information whereby they would have been brought into trouble. We said : Give us a clue ; give us your Impressions, we will take your information confidentially-some things we could not take confidentially but that we could- we will be glad to follow up your clues and ascertain the facts If possible. And I think I shall not be doing wrong if I say that in most cases the gentlemen who thought that there was this widespread fraud are now inclined to believe that they were mistaken. Of course, some thought the restrictions should be greater-I do not say they upheld the whole preferential arrangement ;-but I think that business men are under the impression, not that there are numerous frauds but that the law is being enforced. It may be that there is fraud-there is temptation. But I know on the other hand, that the hon. Minister of Customs has endeavoured to follow up any information he has gained from the merchants. Wherever he has had a clue he has followed it up to ascertain the truth of the case. My hon. friend from Fictou (Mr. Bell) is right in saying that in matters of undervaluation it is the habit of the customs to send agents abroad, if there is reason to believe that any fraud goes on even to a limited extent. It is the duty of the Minister of Customs in such a case, to send out his officers and to see to it that the revenue is protected. While I say with the Minister of Customs that it is possible and even probable that the revenue laws are sometimes evaded, still, my impression is that there is no such general evasion of the British preferential tariff as has been mentioned, and I think that most business men in Canada who have looked into the matter will confirm that impression. If in any case any gentleman in Canada, or any outside of 124*
it, will give information that will enable us to follow up the case, no expense shall be allowed to stand in the way of a full investigation. We have all the same object in view. We all want a British preference, that the article which is the product of British labour shall have the benefit of the British preference. That is why the hon. minister is acting fairly in saying that he would be glad to receive suggestions. When merchants have told me that they believed these evasions were taking place, I have asked them to give us the information and to look into the matter, and they have been compelled to say that they could not give the information and would drop the case. If any merchant in this House or out of it would give us information on which we could proceed, then I believe with the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell), we should follow the matter up and do everything that may be necessary to make the British preference a British preference in reality.

It seems to me that the mistake the hon. Minister of Finance makes is in talking about this as a fraud. If any exporter' has this blank declaration before him what will he do. There are Instructions accompanying it to the customs collector or inspector. And they tell hi nr that in valuing the goods if they are twenty-five per cent in value over the value for which they were sold in the country from which the goods come, then they are to be entered under the preference. If the exporter makes out that declaration and the goods pass, he does not regard it as a fraud. He is complying with the regulations of the law, according to instructions given him from the Customs Department here. So he does not regard it as a fraud and in reality it is not a fraud to him. But it seems to me that the government have arrived at this stage-they admit that the law giving a preference cannot be worked out, that they cannot find ways and means of so working it out as to secure this preference for British goods, yet they will not repeal or amend it, but will allow it to remain as it is and allow this imposition upon the British public and the Canadian public to continue. Because, say they, we do not know how to devise ways and means to carry it out and the opposition will not tell us how to do it. That is about the situation. The hon. Minister of Finance says: that they spoke to reputable business houses. Who were they ? I assume that they are people who buy and import and export this very class of goods and who are interested in carrying on the business exactly upon that line.

If my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) will permit me, what I said was that of the manufacturers who came with a view to obtaining higher duties, if they might, and who suggested their impression that German goods were being brought in under the British prefer-

ence, X have not found one who, when pressed to bring information, could show a single case in which this has taken place.
The hon. gentleman spoke of reputable houses that were consulted in London, England, and the Minister of Customs did the same. If he qualified it by saying manufacturers
The manufacturers I refer to were in Canada.

Have we not shown the minister over and over again how it can be done. Has not the Minister of Customs himself admitted that it could be done in that way ? Yet, with that knowledge before him, he does not propose to amend the law or repeal it, but will allow it to go on.

The Minister of Customs must admit that it is not very easy to allow such a large item as this to pass until he can give a categorical explanation as to what as being done to prevent these frauds. No doubt frauds have been committed-I have myself heard in Montreal time and again cases where the goods were introduced into this country coming from Germany, and without the observation of'the clause in the tariff with which the minister is familiar. So I think we have a right to obtain a clear and categorical statement from the minister, in that voice that can be heard afar, as to what he intends doing to protect the manufacturers of linseed oil, and also what means he intends to adopt to prevent these frauds in the future. The minister must take the House into his confidence. If he is adopting means which he deems it in the public interest not to make public, he is bound to tell us what proportion of this large increase of $80,000 is going to be employed to prevent these frauds. Under these circumstances, I would suggest that this item stand until we have that categorical statement from the minister, to which I think the public are entitled. I move that the committee rise.

Oh, no, Mr. Chairman, not yet. Not only do I want to get these items through to-night, but the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is waiting to get his estimates through. Of course the hon. gentleman is not serious in moving that the committee rise. Perhaps he was not in the House when I was giving categorical answers, as I have been doing all the evening, I have been doing nothing else. He will find my answers in 'Hansard,' and I am sure he will be satisfied with them. But there is not much fraud under the preferential tariff when you compare it with what takes place under the'general tariff. I have admitted there may be fraud, but I go further and I say that under the general tariff I know there'are frauds, lots of them. We know it, because we seize the goods, and we have to adjudicate upon these frauds. We have special officers in Hob. Mr. FIELDING.
the United States who travel about ascertaining the values. Every little while cases are coming before me of frauds which have been going on for three years, where there has been systematic undervaluation during all these years; and in dealing with them we not only make the offenders pay duties for the three years, but we impose'penalties for the three years. There are scores of such cases under the general tariff.
Of fraud ?
Yes, under the general tariff. You must have them, you cannot help it.
Have there heen any seizures in regard to infractions under' the British preference ?

Yes, I believe so ; but there has been nothing like the number that there'is under the general tariff on goods coming from the neighbouring states, where we get all the information we can. There are scores and scores of seizures, always have been and always will be.

The minister says he has officers throughout the United States investigating. How many officers have the government at the present time, or have they had at any time in the past, in the United States, or in England, in Germany, or France ? How many officers have you employed to investigate matters under the British preference ?

We have not had one, nor do I propose going to the expense of sending one until I am more convinced than I am yet that frauds are being perpetrated. I do not believe there is an evasion of the preferential tariff to that extent that would warrant me in having special officers in England to look into the matter.
Are the Americans more dishonest than the Europeans ?

We are doing a large trade with the states, and we have our officers over there. As I say, there have been scores and scores of cases in the department, always have been, of undervaluation and cases of fraud that we have to adjudicate. There is the general tariff, you take what precautions you can. What precautions do you take ? Prima facie, the invoice, then there is the new declaration which I have introduced. The old declaration was ' certified correct.' That was all there was on the invoice. The merchant goes over to the other side and buys goods at 30 per cent discount. The invoice comes in certified correct. It was a perfectly true and honest invoice as between the seller and the purchaser, but it was not correct for the Customs Department, because customs duties are to be levied on the value of the goods when they are sold in that coun-

try. Our merchants were going on and making declarations of the price at which they bought the goods in the country of production. You pointed out to them that the goods were undervalued, and they said they didn't know. Well, we said, there is some one that does know, and that is the man who sells these goods, and we will make him certify to the price, and we got a declaration from him. Now when a case of seizure comes up, we come upon the importer and be says he had no idea the goods were undervalued. But our recourse is not on the foreign merchant, he is not within our reach, but these goods are within our reach, and we put a seizure upon them. It is idle to talk about there being no infringement of the preferential tariff, there may be. but there is nothing approaching the frauds that take place under the general tariff. When I say it is possible that some goods come in illegally, I could not say anything else. But if you want my honest opinion of the preferential tariff. I believe there is very little fraud indeed in comparison with the general tariff. Perhaps I have spoken longer than I should. We want to get on a little faster. We need this money, it is to pay your officers. You believe that your officers ought to be paid a little more, some of them at least ; and we are asking for more money to pay them and to open new ports in order to keep up with the increasing business.

When the minister was in the old country last year he made, as he told us. an effort to find out whether frauds were being committed under this preferential tariff. During the debate a year ago this matter was brought to his attention and a quotation from a British newspaper was read to the House. I propose to read it and find out whether the Minister, when he was in the old country, endeavoured to find out from the publisher of this journal whether this statement was correct.
How Foreigners Rob Canada.
Since Canada granted a preference tariff to Britain, tons upon tons of German and other foreign textiles have been brought over to England and reshipped to Canada, after a so-called process of ' finishing,' in order that they may he classed as goods partly of British manufacture. In some cases this ' finishing ' in England consists simply in taking off the German, French or Austrian labels, doing the goods up again, and then giving them a British name or label. There is no branch of trade in which this style of smuggling is carried on to the extent that it is in the textile trade.- fBelfast ' News,' January 23, 1902.
That was read when this question was up for discussion in the House on a former occasion. When the hon. minister was in the old country surely he would have thought lit worth his while to go and see the publisher of this large and important journal to find out whether he was publishing articles without a tittle of truth in them as the hon. minister has said. Surely he would
have thought it worth his while for the protection of the manufacturers of this country and in view of the complaints that were being made in this House and in the newspapers throughout the country to go to this leading publisher and find out whether this article was correct or not. Surely the hon. minister would have thought it worth his while to put some special officer at work in this country and the old country to find out whether this condition of things could not be stopped in the interests of the people of Canada.
I did not see that article.

It was read in the House last year.
The MINISTER OF CUSTOMS, I did not pay any attention to that article. It is like the criticisms that are rather too strong and which lose their force for that reason. Perhaps there is a possibility that we may be defrauded in some cases under the preferential tariff just as we are under the general tariff, but there could be no better precautions taken than those we have taken that I am aware of, except to employ an army of men over there watching initial processes and then we could not cover every point.
We do not employ any at all.
Well, we had better get on, Mr. Chairman.

We have only touched the fringe of this question and we think a great deal more might be said upon it, particularly since the hon. minister has admitted that he does not employ any special men in Montreal or on the other side to prevent these alleged frauds.
I did not admit that.

This is another of the consequences of this unfortunate preference which has "done no good to the British people and certainly has done no good to us. I would be prepared for my part to allow the item to pass hut the hon. gentleman must understand we cannot go any further this evening.

PrSfontaine), whom we are keeping out of bed to such an unusual hour and who is so unaccustomed to it, but notwithstanding that, now that the hon. Minister of Finance and make him feel that this country is suffering severely as the result of the want of adequate protection to its industries. I contend that we would not have the present disastrous condition of affairs in this country that we regret to see by the Ottawa evening papers to-night had the hon. Minister of Finance taken the proper course at the beginning of this session. If, up to the present time, such serious consequences have resulted from the want of adequate protection to Canadian industries, are we not likely to suffer greater disasters if a change is not brought about ? But, we do hope to have a change. We do not hope to have that change with the present hon. gentlemen in power, but we hope that next year a change will be brought about by the people of this country.
Not much.

I think some hon. gentlemen who say ' not much ' might speak with better knowledge. They know what is going on at the present time in Ontario and in Quebec, and they know how the people are suffering down by the sea. From one end of this country to the other the manufacturers are suffering and suffering definitely and positively in consequence mlL-the manner in which the hon. Minister of Finance has managed the finances and the financial statement of this country. One of the reasons he gave for refusing to make any changes in the tariff this year was that the manufacturers came to him and he refused to accept statements from them which he said they wished to be kept confidential. There was a very good reason for wishing to keep these statements confidential, not from the people of Canada but in the interests of the people of Canada. I think that the hon. Minister of Finance owes the country an apology and the very best reparation he can make after having caused such an enormous loss, and it is no laughing matter-I can assure you it is a very serious matter
That is blue ruin.

To those gentlemen who are handling industrial stocks. The great cry of our hon. friends from the west is wheat. They are all right, but the peiople who are engaged in industrial pursuits, who have invested millions and millions, are losing their money entirely in consequence of the want of proper sympathy and support from the government of this country.

Before that item is passed I would like to get an assurance from the hon. minister in regard to the matter I brought to his attention a little while ago. He is asking for large increases in the salaries of his officers. Surely it would not be too much to ask them to give a receipt when they take money from importers. It is a small matter, but I can assure the hon. minister it is a matter that is felt by those who place their money in the hands of agents at the ports of entry. It is important that they should have a proper means provided of getting a reckoning from these agents. Collusion might take place between the agent and some of the customs officers and a portion of the money in the hands of the broker might be retained. Between the two of them it should be accounted for.

If the hon. gentleman will be kind enough to send me the letter I will correspond with the collector in reference to the matter. It would be inconvenient to make a law like that if there is no general demand for it, and in many of the large ports it would be impossible to do it.
Salaries and contingent expenses of inspectors of ports, and travelling expenses of other offi-

cers on inspection and preventive service ; Board of Customs-expenditure in connection therewith ; Customs laboratory-to meet expenditure in connection with the testing of sugar, molasses, &c., including pay of officers appointed or employed for that purpose ; Salaries of officers appointed or employed for compiling statistical returns of imports and exports, $129,200.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: This item used to be given in detail, under the late government and In the first year of this government, and now we have a lot of these items grouped together and the minister is asking $129,000 for a service that a few years ago used to cost only $40,000. We must have detailed explanation about this.
We really have done a considerable amount of work. We have voted a million dollars now, and we spent the afternoon on the Railway Bill to suit the convenience of the Minister of Railways.
Go on, carried.

These hon. gentlemen need not say ' carried ' because we can stay as long as we see fit to do so. We require an explanation as to why these estimates should be grouped together. I think we have done enough work to-day.
We have done nothing.

Of course, there is no intention to force the committee at all, but I am an old enough parliamentarian to know how part of this discussion has gone on to-night. I know that it is not because of a lack of confidence in the Customs Department or in the officers, but gentlemen opposite are in the mood of enjoying themselves a little. I have been long enough in opposition to understand that. However, there will be an opportunity for that when some of my colleagues bring up their estimates, but mine is a business department. I was asked how long my estimates would take and I said they would go through like a shot because I knew that everything was right. Hon. gentlemen opposite have got up one after another on questions that are not very foreign to the subject although a discussion on the tariff was hardly germane to the estimate. We have got over the troublesome item now, and this is a very easy one. The increase is $8,500, but in the supplementary estimates this year I will have to ask for $6,000, because we were short. Here are the particulars:	Twelve inspectors,
salaries $24,750, expenses $8,500 ; board of customs, 27 officers, salaries $23,500, expenses $7,000 ; statistics, 51 officers, salaries $42,000, expenses $400 ; preventive service, 12 officers, salaries $8,350, expenses $1,300 ; laboratory, 3 officers, salaries $2,900, expenses $2,500-we have to pay express charges on sugar and other articles that are sent to be tested. Of the increase, $6,000
is to meet additions to the staff and in-ireases. Taking out the 12 inspectors and the chief of the preventive service there are 92 officers and an increase of $50 to each of these would mean an increase of $4,600, I am not promising to give the increase, but I am saying what it would be if we did give it, and perhaps the hon. gentleman would not object to that.
Does the hon. gentleman intend to give it ?
I think we will in some cases ; yes.
The minister must have made up his mind to it or he would not ask for more money than he needs.
We are taking a vote for that, and if the hon. gentleman would please let us have it I think we will use it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Why should not these votes be kept distinct and separate as they were in 1897, so that we would know what each costs ? What is the object of mixing them all up together to confuse them ? Omitting this statistical branch which the minister has created, for what purpose we do not know, and which costs $42,000. the minister is now asking $129,200 for services which in 1897 cost us only $42,000.

This has been done for years, and has been sanctioned by the committee, and for the purpose of comparison is all right. The hon. gentleman is mistaken about the expenditure. There is $42,300 for statistics and $8,350 for preventive service which did not exist in 1897. We established it, and. as the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) gave us credit to-night, I believe we have stopped smuggling altogether, and that was a tremendous evil in the province of Quebec and the maritime provinces.
Oh !

I am speaking more particularly of the illicit importations of liquors from St. Pierre and Miquelon, which found their way into those provinces. That is not because the people of those provinces were more addicted to the use of liquor. We have, I believe, wholly stopped that smuggling, and the Minister of Inland Revenue, through that stoppage, finds his receipts greatly increased. The expenditure is against me, but the credit goes to the Department of Inland Revenue.
What amount ?

That I cannot state. Unless the drinking habit is cured, the liquor which was formerly smuggled is now got from the home manufacturer, and the country gets the revenue from it. Then we have increased the inspectors

since 1897. That was necessary to provide for the inspection of ports which had not been inspected for years. With regard to the statistics, the department have been congratulated by the manufacturers of the country for getting them out. We can send to the members and others at their residences, full returns for the previous month, as full as those that appear in the Trade and Navigation returns.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: That is under the Department of Trade and Commerce.

No, by the Customs Department. We publish these returns by the authority of the House. We are taking the vote just as we did before, but we are asking $8,500 to meet the additions to the staff, and leave us a little margin to give an increase of salary to those who deserve it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. gentleman takes credit for establishing the detective service. Surely he cannot take credit for that.
This is the preventive service.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Mr. McMichael was at the head of that service, with a staff of officers under him, and they were paid out of the vote in 1897. And yet the hon. gentleman claims that he established the preventive service. Nothing of the kind; he simply continued the service which he found when he came in, and I do not know that he has added anything to it. The other items were voted separately, whereas my hon. friend grouped them together for his own convenience a year or two ago. It may be that they passed the House unnoticed; but it is not right to vote $129,000 for half a dozen different services. The items should be voted separately so that we shall know what each service costs. My hon. friend claims credit for giving statistical information. We have a double service of that kind both by the Customs Department and the Department of Trade and Commerce. Why should there be this double expenditure unless it is to provide places for friends of my hon. friend.

This preventive service is different from the preventive service to which the hon. gentleman refers. The preventive service we took up, to deal with the great evil of smuggling from St. Pierre and Miquelon.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: We had that before.
No. Mr. Fred Jones was put at the head of that branch, and he and the officers under him have done great work, and the service has paid for itself many times over.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Mr. Jones was not employed. but Mr. McMichael was, and he was at the head of that service.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs

speechtext: Mft McMichael was and is yet at the head of the service. He has inspectors going around to the different ports, but they do not deal with the smuggling. That service is virtually new. The statistics are also new. They are not published by the Department of Trade and Commerce. Every month we send out as fully detailed statistics with reference to the imports and exports of this country as you get in the Trade and Navigation returns, and I can assure the hon. gentleman that they are valued by the business men of Canada, especially by the manufacturers, who have passed resolutions commending me for that course; because it was at their instance largely that these statistics were published.
Are they not published by both the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Customs Department ?

The report of the Department of Trade and Commerce is not in the same shape. They do not give all the details, as we do. What they give they get from the Department of Customs. We gather the information, and they compile it in their own way, in a condensed form.

I would like to get some satisfactory explanation from the hon. minister as to why he has abandoned the former system of giving us these expenses in detail. My hon. friend took nearly ten minutes to explain to us the details of this item of $129,000, which would have been perfectly unnecessary if the estimates had been made as they used to be. I have often observed that the report of the Auditor General in England is far less voluminous than ours, which gives us too much detail. But I maintain that a great deal of our time might be shortened if we had more detail given to us in the estimates submitted by the government. How is it that in former estimates we had all the details that we have been obliged to-night to ask from the minister ?
We had then in former years the amount in each province, the increase in each province, and other details which saved a great deal of discussion. Under the present system the hon. minister may divert one expenditure to another, so that we do not know exactly what we are voting. The hon. minister should alsto explain the distinction between the statistics prepared in the new branch he has organized and those we find in the report of the Department of Trade arid Commerce. I fail to see the difference, and this new department imposes on the country an additional expenditure of $42,000. Why has the hon. minister such an enormous staff in that department ? The country got on very well before without these fifty-one employees, and the hon. minister tells us that he intends increasing the salaries of

these men, who are 'doing just the same work as is done by the Department of Trade and Commerce. We have also a right to know from the hon. minister the names of those whose salaries he intends increasing.

If I gave the names my hon. friend would not be any the wiser, because he does not know the men. The expenditure this year shows an increase of $8,500 over the last. The expenditure last year was $120,700, and the House voted that amount. We need not therefore go behind that. We have that as a basis to start from, because the House sanctioned that last year, but lion, gentlemen have a right to ask for the details of this additional expenditure of $8,500.
The conditions may be changed from last year.

The only change is that we are asking a little more salary for some of the men employed in this work, I think it is a fair rule of criticism that you should start with that amount voted last year as a basis, and ask for details of the additional sum required.
The hon. gentleman need not tell us what policy we should follow in criticising his estimates.
I was simply pointing out what I judged to be legitimate criticism.
We are the best judges of that.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. minister says that the opposition admitted that the vote of $120,000 last year was right. But he will find that the opposition objected as strongly to that vote then as they do now. But because we do not give an individual or separate vote on each item and because an item is forced through by the majority behind him, the hon. minister taunts us with having admitted that the $120,000 voted last year was necessary. We did not admit it then nor do we admit it now, and I would move to have the item reduced by this $8,500.
If you move to reduce this, you are going to place it out of my power to give any additional sum to men I consider underpaid.

Not at all, because under the system adopted by the hon. gentleman he can take the money from another part and increase the salaries. He is not bound by this item. The hon. gentleman has not answered any of my questions. I asked why he has abandoned the system of giving the various items composing this vote. We then could tell for what specific purpose we were voting the money. But to-day, instead of giving us the vote under a number of different heads, he groups it in one single item of $120,000, which will enable him to
| distribute the whole sum of money over the I different heads as he chooses. We are asked to vote $120,000 for seven or eight different objects without knowing what amount will be devoted to each one. There may be reason for that. Surely the hon. minister is able to give us the reason. Otherwise, we shall pursue that course and, in future years we shall be voting still larger sums en bloc without knowing what amount is to be devoted to each separate item. That is contrary to the principle of voting money that we have usually followed and are still following in other matters. As representatives of the people we ought to vote the money for each separate item and limit the sum to that item. This is a wise rule that we have followed, and it is the rule followed in England, and, so far as I know, in the United States, and in the large budget that is voted in France. There may be a reason why we should not follow that rule, but, if so, why does the minister not state it ? Another question which I asked, which the minister did not attempt to answer. I merely wanted to draw attention to the difference, if any, between the expensive statistical branch he has established and the one in the department of Trade and Commerce, which formerly gave us the same information. There has been no answer. Was the hon. gentleman himself when in opposition, satisfied with those on the treasury benches when they did not answer his questions ? I have never bad the pleasure of seeing the hon. gentleman perform the duties of a member of the opposition, but I am sure that he insisted upon answers to his reasonable questions. Then the hon. minister will observe that he has not given us the names of those whose salaries are to be increased, for which purpose he asked a considerable amount. Why not give these names ? I think we have a right to answers to these questions, and I would like the hon. minister to give me that satisfaction before we pass this item.
I said to the hon. gentleman that for years the estimates have been prepared in this way.
Not in 1890.

It has been so for some years. It is more convenient. If the items were specified, you would not be able to do with the officers of the department what you can now. The services are of like nature-as, for instance, the inspector of the preventive service, the statistical branch and the laboratory. You cannot estimate exactly what you are going to want for each service. But, in this way of voting the money, you can interchange the officers as you could not do otherwise and pass the Auditor General if the money were otherwise voted. You might want to take an officer of the statistical branch and assign him to the board of customs or one in the office of the board of customs and put him in the preventive service or the labor-

atory or make one of them assistant inspector. As changes become necessary during the year you can make them. It will be more than a year before this vote is expended. and it is impossible to say what changes may be necessary in that time.

Why should the hon. minister make any such changes ? _ The hon minister will pardon me for saying that it is incredible that he sould need to distribute his officers in this way. Does he say that he has a staff of officers compiling statistics for whom he has hot employment during the year ? If so he bad better dismiss them. And so with the other branches. It is unreasonable that the hon. gentleman should bulk five or six distinct services and ask the House to vote the whole sum. The country will expect him to tell how much he needs for travelling expenses of inspectors. how much for travelling expenses for other officers, how much for the board of customs, how much for the laboratory, and so on. Each of these is a distinct service. The hon. gentleman will concede that there is nothing unfair in that. I hope bis answer will not be that the item slipped through in other years and that therefore it should be passed now. The fact that it slipped through without question before does not do away with the right of the 'committee to ask for the facts now. Will he give his estimate of how much is required for each service ? If he cannot, he has bungled his department and its expenditure in sueh an extraordinary manner that the country cannot learn anything about it.
I gave that detail, but the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) did not hear it.
Did the hon. gentleman give it for each service ?
Yes, and I have no objection to repeating the figures for the information of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy).
I understood the hon. gentleman to give the estimate for last year. But, of course, that is only half the- question. Will he give the expenditure ?
That is the actual expenditure for 1901-2.

I think that, so far ns getting any information from the hon. gentleman in regard to the difference between his statistical branch and the similar branch in the Department of Trade and Commerce, I must give it up.

No, 1 must beg the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Monk's) pardon. I was going on to speak of that, when the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Claney) interrupted me. If the hon. member for Jacques Cartier can bring that up when the Minister of Trade and Commerce is putting his estimates through, the Minis-Hon. Mr. FITZPATRICK.
ter of Trade and Commerce will then give Ills reasons for the publication that comes from his department. I have given the justification for the issue so far as the Customs Department is concerned. I believe every member of the House values this publication. By bringing the statistical department here we are able to do what we could not do before. We used to have great delay in obtaining the Trade and Navigation returns. Sometimes, even in the month of March, we could not get the returns of the imports and exports of Canada for the month of .Tune previously. Members were forced to ask for special returns, whereas under this system, in the month of .July, you can get the whole transactions, imports and exports, for the month of June.

I do not quite see that the statements which we get should necessitate so large a staff of employees. Here are fifty of them at an expenditure of over ?40,000 a year. I can understand that possibly a larger number of employees might get out the information more rapidly than we got it before.

The hon. gentleman will be pleased to know that our statistical department is doing its work very rapidly. There is not a country on the face of the globe that gets out as prompt returns and with as much information as we get. I believe Canada stands ahead of every nation in this respect.

I do not at all agree with the hon. gentleman. It is like our Yearbook that we get a year after the proper time. If you go to New Zealand, to Australia, or to all the other British dependencies, you will find that their Year-book is out a long time before ours. If you go to the United States, you will find that their statistical abstracts of trade are more complete, sooner brought out, better printed, in fact better than ours in every respect. But the hon. gentleman, I think, has laid down a very erroneous principle when he claimed that because we had passed an item in a previous year we must necessarily pass it every year, unless there is an increase. I do not think the hon. gentleman adhered to that principle when he was in opposition. Parliament is called expressly for the purpose of criticising every year every item of expenditure ; that is our duty, and we are endeavouring to fulfil it. Now when my hou. friend to my right made a motion to reduce this item by $8,500, he gave us an example of the kind of arbitrary power we are conferring upon the minister. What did the minister say ? He said that in that case all the poor employees of his department would be deprived of their increase of salary for this year. What enabled the hon. gentleman to say that ? Just the very rule which he has infringed for two or three years past, and which my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor) pointed out. He gave

us several services voted en bloc; and then he says that he can Increase or diminish the number of members of the board of customs and their travelling expenses. He is absolute master of that sum of $129,000. My hon. friend knows what difficulties this government had with the Auditor General, most of which were based upon the failure to observe the good old rule that we should vote specific amounts for specific purposes. Now I venture to say that most of the correspondence that we find in the Auditor General's Report since this wise rule has been infringed, has been caused precisely by a failure to observe that rule. Under 'this particular vote let me point out that we can diminish the salary of all the employees of the board of customs out of the $24,000 that he says is required for that special service for this year. Out of that $24,000 he can divert any sum he likes, to provide for the expenses of a preventive service, for instance. Does he not see that voting money in that way deprives the House of Commons of its valuable privilege of controlling these expenses ? We say to the minister :	Here is a sum of $129,000,
of which you can spend just as much as you like, provided you confine it to six or seven specific objects. If I am in order, Mr. Chairman, I move that this item 228, of $129,200, be divided so as to show the sum of money to be appropriated to each service. I think that would be bringing us back to a very wise rule, and save the government a good deal of trouble with the Auditor General.

That is the only safe rule parliament can follow in voting money. Tlie object of separating it up into as many parts as possible is that the House may understand what the money is needed for, and afterwards that there may be control over its expenditure.
The MINISTER <3f CUSTOMS. I trust hon. gentlemen do not think it necessary to do that. Where is the danger ? If there be no danger, it is a convenience in the department. If I had to estimate for these different votes I should then have to estimate for a larger amount than I am asking here. I would have to ask for more money under different heads. Things will occur. There are fourteen months ahead before some of this money will be expended, and it is impossible to estimate the whole thing. As it is, this is in the hands of the minister, and it will be in the hands of the minister then. The minister has no more opportunity of doing what is unjust if the vote were divided than he has now. When you want to make an expenditure of a certain amount for a public work, you want to know how much money you are going to expend and what it is for. This is an absolutely different thing, because we are now dealing with the question of salaries and expenses attendant upon the duties of these men.
Under the old system, when it was broken up and specifically given, was it the custom of the government to ask for more ? They asked for less.

I will give the hon. gentleman an illustration of that myself. Formerly the vote was made by provinces. This was changed, because you could not estimate fourteen months ahead, and you would have to make an outside estimate for each province. If you ran short $2,000 in one province and you had $S,000 which you did not need in another province, you could not, under the old system, use the unexpended money in the province where your estimate had fallen short, and the officers in the province in which you were short would hav.e to wait for their pay until the new estimates were passed.
If the House votes money for, say the board of customs, the hon. minister asks the privilege of being allowed to expend that on salaries. Would he not regard that as dangerous legislation ?
The board of customs means salaries.
Or for travelling expenses. The hon. minister has a general vote here, and he can take that money and apply it to-any purpose he wishes.
Within the vote.
Is that not a rather dangerous kind of legislation ? I think it is, and it is not permitted in any other department of government.
Oh, yes ; that has always been permitted in the estimates of the Inland Revenue Department.
Not in the estimates of the Minister of Public Works.
That isa very different thing.

It is a question whether this House has a right to pass legislation in that way. It seems to me that the minister having charge of that department in the House ought to be able to say nearly how much money he requires for the next twelve or fourteen months for the payment of salaries.
That is-what I am doing.
And that he should be able to say what he requires for travelling expenses.
That is what I have done.
Then, if the hon. minister comes forward and says that he wants $20,000 for travelling expenses, what objection can he have to saying that it will be expended for that purpose alone ?

speakerposition: topic

speechtext: You cannot tell exactly. Suppose a case of fraud arises and a special officer has to go to Kansas City,-or New York, or Philadelphia, or Boston, you must have a little something to play on. If I had to separate this, I would have to ask for a larger amount than I have, because there would be a danger that in some way we might be short, and the expenses could not be paid. The mission would have to be foregone or the officer could not get his pay. I have given the actual expenses under the different heads last year.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: How much did they amount to 7
$121,000. There is nothing to be gained by dividing the vote, and you will only make it more difficult for the department to work. You will just increase the book-keeping.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: How would it increase the book-keeping 7

Let us take the hon. minister's reasoning, and we could very much reduce the work of this House. Take, for instance, the Militia Department. There is money to be voted for cartridges, for travelling expenses,- pay and drill. We have been dividing these items up and asking for a specific amount for each of them. We could reduce the work very materially by saying we want $2,500,000 for militia purposes. We might go through every department of government and do the same thing. But we do not do it, because parliament, in its wisdom, has devised a better way, and one that is calculated more to protect the public treasury.	'
Mr. CLANCY, How is the minister able to say what each service costs if there is that promiscuous sort of a thing, of one clerk going from one service to the other. How often has that happened during the past year.
I am told T>y the accountant that we have done it two or three times during the last two or three months.

The very rarity of its occurrence shows that there is no necessity for it. The minister was an able critic when in opposition and he did his country good service, but he knows that such a latitude amounts to license and that it is an extremely bad precedent. I am prepared to acquit the hon. gentleman of anything like stealing or misappropriating any money or anything of that kind, because I believe that if a greater sum were voted to him than is necessary he would only spend so much as would be in the interest of the country, but the principle is wrong.

There is no parallel between this case and the case Mr. BLAIN.
of the Department of Public Works' as has been cited. It would not be right to take a vote of $2,000,000 for buildings in Ontario without specifying where these buildings were, but here is a vote to pay salaries earned by our officers and what does it matter so long as the salary is paid whether it is paid under the head of statistics or under the head of Board of Customs. It is a convenience to the department and I hope hon. gentlemen will let it pass, as it is now nearly one o'clock.

I move to amend the second item of resolution on 228 so as to show the the sum of money to be appropriated to each service. I am quite prepared to admit that I believe the minister will make a judicious use of this money and that he will not divert it unnecessarily from one service to the other, but in order to defend this system he should not fall back upon his own honesty in which we have the most implicit trust. There is no such vote as this taken in committee of the British parliament.
My impression is that the whole army vote and navy vote is passed in a bulk sum.
No.
I am inclined to think so, but I am very certain there is no such detail in the British estimates as there is in our estimates.

I am perfectly sure that the hon. gentleman is mistaken when he says that the whole army vote or the whole navy vote in England is passed in a bulk sum. We never find in the British estimates a number of items accumulated together as these are. In voting this sum of $139,000, we are confiding the disposal of it to the hon. gentleman's own discretion. That is what we have no right to do.. My hon. friend says he would probably not make any undue use of the money, even in the exercise of that discretion. But in all previous years up to 1896, we voted the amount for the service under separate items. In 1896 it amounted to $819,000, whereas here it amounts to $1,000,000, all the items being grouped together.
Amendment negatived : Yeas, 7 ; nays, 28.
Might I ask the hon. min-nister if he proposes to establish a customhouse in Bracebridge 7

Brace-n-idge is one of fifteen or twenty po uts with reference to which applications have been made. It is an important point, and the application is under consideration. We have not yet finally determined. We ascertain in all cases what business is done. I had a deputation to see me about Bracebridge.
I might ask about Dresden 7
It is under i consideration, too.

May I ask the hon. gentleman if there is any comfort to be drawn from the fact that it is under consideration ? Does that brighten the present prospect any ? He took Dresden under consideration last year, when he asked for $10,000 for matters of this kind, including, I believe, some service in British Columbia. This year he is asking for a larger sum. The country has a fair claim on the large revenue the hon. gentleman is collecting from the people, and I think he ought to congratulate himself that there are not more than twenty places asking for additional advantages. I quite understand that the hon. gentleman is subject to constant pressure, in some cases not entirely warranted. I also recognize that it is difficult to make a distinction between different places; but there are always business interests, as in the town of Dresden, which should decide the matter, and the people there put to inconvenience in not having that point made an outport. The hon. gentleman has a preventive officer at Walpole Island, and I would suggest that he might transfer that officer to Dresden and do away with the service at Walpole Island. I know the locality very well. It is said that smuggling has gone on there to a large extent; but a very small sum is collected by the officer there, indicating that the smuggling is very small. I hope the hon. gentleman will consider the desirability of making this change.

It was represented that there was a large Indian settlement at Walpole Island, and that there was not only smuggling, but that the Indians were getting liquor, and that it was desirable to have an officer there. Dresden is becoming an important point. Brace-bridge is also. As the hon. gentleman knows, Dresden is near Wallaceburg.
Twelve miles distant.

That would weigh against it as compared with Bracebridge, whose nearest point is Orillia, thirty-five miles away. I am not putting one place against the other. I am merely stating the points that we have to consider.

I would like to know where the hon. gentleman gets the representation that the Indians are bringing in liquor to such an extent as to require him to keep an officer there. It is not liquor to resell. If it is a little bottle in an Indian's pocket, the officer would have as much difficulty as anybody else in protecting iit. I would like to know where the representation comes from.
I do not know whether it was an inspector or not who reported it, but it was reported that it was necessary.

I would like to call attention to the reports I have heard of frauds in Montreal in connection with importations from Germany. The hon. minister might employ somebody to find out whether those reports, which have reached me from reputable people, are well founded.
Miscellaneous-Day books, ledgers, bookbinding, printing and stationery, subscriptions to commercial papers, flags, dating stamps, locks, instruments, &,c., for various ports of entry,, legal expenses and uniforms for customs officers, $37,500.

There is an increase of $2,500 here, which is required to meet the cost of printing a book now in course of preparation by the assistant commissioner, containing instructions to the customs officers on tlieir respective dutiCjS. We have 1,617 officers, and I suppose each one should have a copy.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: How does the hon. minister account for requiring $37,500 now when in 1896-7 only $15,000 were required.
$3,000 are accounted for by the expenditure on uniforms.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I find by the Auditor General's Report that last year the department purchased from W. E. Charleson, goods to the amount of $784.94. Were those purchased by tender ?
TJie MINISTER OF CUSTOMS. No, they were just small items.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: They were small items bought at retail prices. There is no merchant in Canada who figures so often in the Auditor General's Report as W. G. Charleson. In this account, F-36 of the Auditor General's Report, there are sixteen coal screens at $7.75; enamelled measures, two sets $9.50; ever-ready flash lights, two, $7.50; hammers and hatchets, twenty-four at fifty cents, three at sixty cents; nail pullers, one at $1.25, fourteen at $1.50. In any hardware store you can purchase the best at one dollar. We want samples of these goods brought here. Paper clips, 101, $75.75; padlocks, two gross at $125. We would like to see a sample of the padlocks. You can buy them at ninety cents a piece.

We want good padlocks.
Mr. TAYLOR, Yes, and I know what customs padlocks are. Why not go to a wholesale hardware man and pay cash prices instead of paying Charleson retail prices for two gross of padlocks, $250. Scales, union, three at $7; four at $7.50; special, seventeen at $6, one at $7; stamping scales, $7.65; small items, $38.40. These goods are charged from twenty-five to fifty per cent advance on the wholesale price. Why should the hon. minister throw away the people's

money in this manner ? I think this is enough to warrant the committee to be careful in voting money to the minister-in whose own honesty every person has confidence, but whose department we find buying articles from Mr. Charleson at such prices as I have quoted.

This is something I do not know about. To tell the truth I did not know that Mr. Charleson's name was there. But I am glad the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) has mentioned the matter. I do not know that we can buy these small articles by tender, but we have a right to be saved from over-charge. I will take this matter up with the clerk of supplies and shall question him as to whether we get proper value. So far as I am concerned, I want no extra prices paid for goods, I will look into the matter.
I see that legal expenses are included in this item. How much was spent for legal expenses last year ?
There were only two small items, one for legal advice given to the collector at Montreal, $12 odd, and the other was over some trouble about a lease in Richibucto.

This is another case of grouping. And, to show that in England these items are voted according to the principles we have been defending, let me point out the difference. This item includes : day-books, ledgers, book-binding, printing and stationery, subscriptions to commercial papers, flags, dating stamps, locks, &c., for various ports of entry, legal expenses and uniforms for customs officers. In England they separate printing, paper, parchments, binding, small stores, printing for stationery, office publications. There is far more detail in England and each item is treated separately.
Is not the army estimate put through in one vote ?

I have not the army vote here, but the hon. gentleman may be quite sure that in England money is not voted in this way. Now, with regard to the point raised by my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor), why does not the department adopt the principle which is observed in England and which I have often advocated here ? In England they send out a circular with respect to stationery and other articles which! the department may require. A list of the articles is given, and the circular is sent to responsible persons, who are asked to report the lowest price at which they will furnish these articles. But the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Paterson) purchases these articles without tender, and without information as to prices from friends of the department. We lose more money in that way than it would take to put the port of Montreal in perfect condition in five years. Is the hon. gentleman willing to try the ex-Mr. TAYLOR.
periment of following the English fashion in this matter ?
Day books, ledgers, stationery and such articles are furnished to all the departments from the Printing Bureau.

Why is not the principle adopted for all the departments ? The hon. gentleman knows that at present when hardware is required, it is Mr. Charleson who sells it to the government at prices that are always or almost always excessive. We have gone into these details in the Public Accounts Committee, and in every case there was proof that a great deal more was charged than the regular price.
I think that is a mistake.

No, I think the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Fielding) will recollect seeing in his own newspaper organs, statements that we were paying attention to trifles. They were trifles taken separately, but the aggregate of all these trifles was a very large sum. But, not only is it a loss of money, but the,system is unjust to the people in the trade. Under the method pursued in England every man has an equal chance to sell his goods to the government.
It seems to me that this new arrangement is an ingenious device to get around the Auditor General who has been a very troublesome official to the government-
Not to our departmeht.

Reading the correspondence in the Auditor General's Report, I think we are justified in coming to that conclusion. He has objected to expenditure in many cases because it was not, in his judgment, in acordance with the purpose for which the money was voted. Now, this new arangement is the only way-except by over-' ruling by the Treasury Board-by which the government can get over the Auditor General. This is admirably calculated to answer the purpose and leave the government free to spend money in any one of half a dozen lines without any check whatever. We have just voted a sum of no less than $129,200 which may be spent on travelling expenses, board of customs laboratory, or statistical branch. No matter how the government arranges the expenditure within these broad limits, the Auditor General can make no complaint. If this system is to be continued, you might as well do away with the Auditor General, for his supervision of expenditure is reduced practically to nothing. I do not believe the country will endorse this or like it. The Auditor General is a most useful and important officer, and his power of imposing a check upon the government expenditure should not be curtailed. The sooner we drop this system and revert to that which we

formerly had, the better. We asked the minister several, times why he grouped the expenditures in this way, and he gave us several frivolous reasons-did not appeal to us as being legitimate or proper reasons at all. I think I can see through it plainly now, that is the reason for which it has been adopted. I think we will find many evils creeping in under this system, and the sooner we abandon it the better.
But they do not discuss individual items as the hon. gentleman is doing.
If we take a longer time to vote the estimates, it is because we do not have the information.
The item under consideration is word for word as it was in 1895-96.
That does not make it right.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will certainly allow this item to stand until he brings down the information.
No.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Then we can stay here as long as the hon. gentleman can. My hon. friend said he did not know that Mr. Charleson spent 8780 of this money last year buying goods. He says the storekeeper no doubt did it. But storekeepers only buy at such places as the government directs. I presume the minister tells his storekeeper where he shall buy his supplies.
No, I do not, the commissioner may.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman allow this item to stand until he brings down the information, telling us where the storekeeper purchased these goods and at what prices ? And let him give us some illustration of the values that we get for the money we expend.
He purchased them because he wanted them, and he certifies to all of them as being reasonable.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Let us have a sample of the goods. We have men in this House who know the value of goods as well as Mr. Charleson. The hon. gentleman does not know anything about the value of these goods.
He certifies that the prices are fair and just. I told the hon. gentleman that I would look into it myself, if that is what he means.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Then bring down the information before the item is passed.
On concurrence. I cannot get it to-night. I am anxious to get this passed, so that we may pay these men.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: We can stay till six o'clock, and we are prepared to do it. The hon. gentleman is undertaking to bluff us to-night. He wants to pass all his estimates before he quits. He is not going to make any progress by adopting this course. Though we are few in numbers, we have just as strong powers of endurance as the hon. gentleman and his friends. We want some more information. Will the hon. geu-tleman bring down a sample of these goods and submit them to members of this House who are acquainted with the prices ? He will find that the prices are outrageous.
Can you not criticise these items in the Public Accounts Committee ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: But the minister is asking for these votes for next year, and probably a slice of them will go to Mr. Charleson again.
The accountant tells me that he cannot get a nail puller, that they have not got any.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Your accountant will not tell you that he cannot get a duplicate of them.

1 know what an opposition can do if they want to. But when the hon. gentleman says he will talk till daylight, I do not think his friends will support him. The hon. gentleman says lie thinks that we paid excessive prices for certain supplies. Well, I will take care to examine into that, I will do so to-morrow the first thing. I will have the clerk of supplies up, and find out what he has done. Now the accountant tells me that he gets a statement that the goods have been received and that the prices charged are fair and just. This person was not appointed by me. He is one of the higher salaried officers and a cousin of Sir Charles Tupper, I think, but a gentleman we have confidence in, and when the hon. gentleman says that they will talk all night unless I consent to let this go, I do not think he is reasonable. This item we are considering now has been the same year after year, with the exception that the customs officer's uniform has been added.

I do not think there is anything unreasonable in this demand. Here is an item of $37,000 which is not as it has been in previous years. It is more than

doubled, and we And that Mr. Charleson has sold to the government an item of $708 worth of goods. I am not an expert in the value of hardware. My hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) is, and perhaps the hon. minister is, and perhaps he will be struck with the prices that are charged in that account. They appear to be very abnormal and very extravagant and this is not the first time Mr. Charleson's name has come under the observation of this committee, and the Committee on Public Accounts in connection with excessive charges.
A customs lock would necessarily be a good lock.
Is there anything unreasonable in asking that we should see samples of this extravagant bill of sale?
These goods are scattered all over the country.
There are no samples ?
No samples, so the accountant tells me.
As my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) says they could be got at any time, and one of these locks would be worth keeping as a curiosity.
This clerk can go before the Public Accounts Committee.
When we have voted the money and find that these remarkable charges have been made, our duty is to recriminate.
Would the hon. gentleman know the value of a padlock if he were to see it ?

I would. But there are other articles mentioned that I do not know very much about, and I would certainly like to see these samples. I do not think this is a very unreasonable demand. I venture once more to make an appeal to the hon. leader of the House. It is going on to two o'clock and I do not think it is fair to ask us to sit here any longer. I am ready to remain all night if it is necessary.

I had hoped at an earlier stage of the evening that we might have had an opportunity of directing our attention to the estimates of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Prcfontnine). but it is rather too late now for that. I think, however, that having devoted so much time to the estimates of the hon. Minister of Customs, it is only reasonable that we should finish this branch of the estimates and then adjourn. In regard to the late hours, my own opinion is that if the session is to close any time this side of October we will have to sit later than we have been doing in the past. I hope to have the co-operation of hon. gentlemen opposite. It is all very well to adjourn at eleven o'clock if business is going Mr. MONK.
on smoothly, but if the work is to be disposed of it will be necessary that we should sit later than we have been doing in the past.

I agree with the hon. Minister of Finance as to the desirability of finishing the session, but it seems to me that we are called upon too early in the session to vote large sums of money when Important measures are left in abeyance until it is too late to do them justice. Now, as to the proposition of my hon. friend may I suggest to him that we finish these estimates of the Department of Customs with the exception of one item, the amount required to meet the expenditure in the Yukon. I make this request as there are really so few of us here to-night, and I think it would be well to leave one item open.

There are supplementary estimates for the current year and the coming year to come down, and I can assure the hon. gentleman that they will afford ample opportunity for discussing customs matters, and that if they pass this item they will not in any way deny themselves the opportunity of discussing any customs questions at a later stage If in their judgment such is necessary.
The MINISTER OF CUSTOM^. I have to bring down supplementary estimates for the Yukon for this year, and hon. gentlemen will then have an opportunity of discussing the question because there will be an expenditure made.
I suppose if we have an opportunity in the Public Accounts Committee to look into this account of Mr. Charleson we can bring it up in the supplementary estimates ?

I have not the slightest objection to you doing it?
Amount required to meet expenditure in ftie Yukon Territory, $40,000.
The hon. minister ought to give us some explanation as to the increase because there has been a falling off in the revenue.
Not this year.
As compared with two years ago.

We ask $40,000 for 1903-4. For the current year we asked $31,000, and I will have to bring down a supplementary estimate for $5,000 extra for this year so that the actual increase will be $4,000 over the expenditure of the current year.
What is the cause of the increase ? As the hon. Postmaster General (Hon. Sir Wm. Mulock) knows there has been a very great shrinkage in the revenue.

I will have to ask for a supplementary estimate

this year for $5,000 more, so that really when this is voted by the House the increase will be $4,000, as between 1902-3 and 1903-4. The increase is made up by an increase in living expenses of two officers at Dawson. Messrs. Harold Rolph and A. Forest, of from $1,200 to $1,800 per year each, increased living allowance to the appraiser, Mr. Wm. Merchant, from $1,200 to $1,800. That is for six months. He comes out from the Yukon to Victoria during the winter, and he is not allowed his living expenses then, but for the six months he is in the Yukon he is allowed $1,800. Then, we have a new officer, Mr. A. D. Ross, who has no living allowance, but who has a salary of $1,800, and there are two new officers who are employed seven months in the year at a salary of $150 a month each. They are T. W. Alcock and T. R. Moulton. These officers were employed on the recommendation of Chief Officer McMichael. He went up there during the summer clothed with plenary power to put the office in perfect shape and he made these arrangements. Some resolutions reported.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved the adjournment of the House.

I beg to call the attention of the government to the following telegram which I have received :
Some men interested in cattle trade called on me to-night and asked me to put in protest against government's Bill insisting on the stamping of hides. They say there should be no government interference in the matter, for instance, if their hides are stamped number three by the government inspector and they cannot get their price here and have to sell in the states the stamp will hurt them very much. Look into the matter and if you can say something in above line try and do so as I hear also it is the tanners who are at the bottom of it and against the cattle men and farmers.
This telegram is from Mr. W. F. Maclean.
I understand the Bill is before the sub-committee and not finally considered, and I wish to call the attention of the government to it, so that they may know. Might I ask what business will be taken up to-morrow ?
The Minister of Railways desires to resume the consideration of the Railway Bill.
Will that be all for tomorrow ?
If we get through that we will, be very glad ; the Bill is quite a long one.
If you get through will you go into supply ?
I did not anticipate that we would get through with it, but if we should be so fortunate as to dispose of it-
If you dispose of that, will you go into supply ? It is of some importance that we should know.

It is possible we might take up other Bills, but if all other business is disposed of, we would have to go on with supply, and in that case the estimates of the Minister of Marine will be under consideration.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 1.50 a.m., Wednesday.
